articles.title: This 3900-Hectare Nickel-Copper-Cobalt Acquisition Comes With Big Unanswered Question - Streetwise Reports
articles.summary: This 3900-Hectare Nickel-Copper-Cobalt Acquisition Comes With Big Unanswered Question  Streetwise Reports
articles.full_text:
Key Investor Takeaways
- Copper One Resources Corp. has agreed to acquire a 100% interest in the Sword & Gossan nickel-copper-cobalt properties in Labrador for CA$3.65 million in purchase consideration, plus CA$400,000 in scheduled advance royalty payments, bringing total scheduled cash commitments to CA$4.05 million and expanding its North American critical metals exploration portfolio.
- The 3,900-hectare Sword & Gossan property includes 156 mineral claims covering a historically explored nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide system, with multiple untested electromagnetic conductors, surface mineralization, and historical drill intercepts.
- Copper One's flagship Majuba Hill copper project in Nevada has undergone more than 90,000 feet of drilling across more than 100 holes. The company expanded its planned 2026 Phase 2 diamond drilling program to up to 10,000 feet to test priority targets and advance the project toward a maiden mineral resource estimate.
- AI-assisted copper exploration at Majuba Hill uses ExploreTech geological modeling to identify drilling targets. The company's 2025 drilling included an AI-designed hole that intersected copper mineralization associated with the South Resistivity Anomaly.
- Copper One's 2026 exploration milestones include advancing Phase 2 drilling at Majuba Hill, evaluating priority breccia targets, refining its three-dimensional geological model, and continuing work toward a maiden NI 43-101-compliant mineral resource estimate.
Copper One Expands Critical Minerals Portfolio With CA$3.65 Million Labrador Acquisition
Copper One Resources Corp. (CEXY:CSE; CEXYF:OTCPK; IW8:FSE) announced that it had entered into a purchase and sale agreement to acquire a 100% interest in the Sword & Gossan Mineral Properties in west-central Labrador, Newfoundland and Labrador.
The agreement, dated October 6, 2026, was entered into with 1594122 B.C. Ltd., an arm's-length vendor. The acquisition covers ten mineral licenses comprising 156 claims across approximately 3,900 hectares, located about 90 kilometers north of Churchill Falls on the northern side of the Smallwood Reservoir.
The property includes the historical Sword, also known as Michikamau, nickel-copper-cobalt project, where previous operators conducted airborne geophysical surveys, geological mapping, surface sampling, and initial drilling. That work identified a magmatic sulphide system containing nickel-copper-cobalt mineralization, along with multiple electromagnetic conductors that have not been drill-tested.
The central unanswered question is whether the electromagnetic conductors identified at Sword & Gossan represent substantial nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide mineralization. Although historical reports described mineralized showings and drilling that intersected sulphides at the Juno conductive zone, most of the property's electromagnetic targets remain untested by drilling. Additional exploration, laboratory analysis, and geological evaluation will be required to determine whether these targets contain mineralization of sufficient grade, size, and continuity to warrant further development studies.
"The proposed acquisition of Sword & Gossan would expand Copper One's North American critical metals portfolio with a nickel-copper-cobalt exploration opportunity in Labrador," said David Greenway, President and CEO of Copper One, in the company's news release. "Historical surface sampling and drilling identified mineralization, while multiple electromagnetic conductors remain untested."
Under the agreement, Copper One will pay the vendor CA$3.65 million in cash, consisting of an initial CA$1.15 million payment due one business day after the agreement's effective date and a second payment of CA$2.5 million within six months of execution. In addition, the company is required to make two advance royalty payments of CA$200,000 each on the first and second anniversaries of the effective date, bringing total scheduled cash commitments to CA$4.05 million, excluding any optional royalty buyback. No company securities will be issued as part of the acquisition.
The property is subject to an existing 2% net smelter returns royalty payable to its underlying owner. Copper One has the option to purchase 1% of that royalty for CA$2 million in cash at any time through written notice, reducing the aggregate royalty to 1%.
Completion of the transaction remains subject to due diligence, board approvals, required third-party consents, Canadian Securities Exchange acceptance, and the absence of a material adverse change in the property's status before closing. No finder's fees are payable.
The Sword project area consists of seven licenses covering 57 claims and 1,425 hectares, while Gossan comprises three licenses covering 99 claims and 2,475 hectares. The vendor has represented that the licenses are in good standing, with CA$31,200 in assessment expenditures due between July and August 2027.
The property lies within the Michikamau Intrusion, one of Labrador's largest anorthosite-troctolite intrusive complexes, and approximately 300 kilometers southwest of the Voisey's Bay nickel-copper-cobalt mine.
Historical exploration conducted between 2005 and 2007 identified multiple electromagnetic conductors that geophysical consultants interpreted as potentially consistent in intensity and geometry with massive sulphide bodies. Most remain untested by drilling. Copper One cautioned in its October 7, 2026, announcement that a qualified person had not completed sufficient work to verify the historical exploration results and that the company was not treating them as current. The historical interpretations and electromagnetic anomalies do not establish the presence, grade, continuity, or economic viability of mineralization.
Historical surface prospecting reported nickel, copper, and cobalt mineralization at several gossanous showings, including Gossan 115 and Sword Far North. At the Juno conductive zone, a historical two-hole drilling program reportedly intersected nickel-copper-cobalt sulphide mineralization across a broad interval. The previous operator's assessment report recommended deeper drilling to investigate a possible feeder system.
The conductors occur within troctolite and leuco-troctolite host rocks, which previous geological interpretations associated with a possible feeder zone to the Michikamau Intrusion.
Copper, Nickel, and Cobalt Markets Reflect Shifting Supply and Demand
According to Trading Economics on October 13, copper traded at US$6.7148 per pound, up 0.24% for the day, 6.08% over the previous month, and 35.05% year over year. The publication reported that copper futures had climbed toward US$6.70 per pound, approaching record highs amid supply disruptions in Chile, the world's largest copper producer.
On the demand side, increased orders associated with data centers, semiconductor development, artificial intelligence infrastructure, battery storage, and electric vehicles across Asia continued to support the market outlook. Falling oil prices also provided support by potentially easing inflationary pressures and reducing expectations for aggressive U.S. Federal Reserve monetary tightening.
Trading Economics on October 8 described cobalt as a "hard, lustrous, gray metal with a high melting point (1493°C)." Its reported applications included chemicals, superalloys for gas turbine blades and aircraft engines, specialized steel, carbides, diamond tools, and magnets. Chemical production accounted for approximately 58% of cobalt use, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo represented more than half of global production.
In its nickel market commentary, Trading Economics reported that "Nickel fell to around US$15,600 per tonne, hitting its lowest level since December 2025 as ample availability continued to weigh on prices."
The report identified increased Philippine nickel ore shipments to Indonesia and rising London Metal Exchange inventories as factors contributing to available supply. Exchange inventories had climbed to 278,898 tonnes by September 24 from an August low of 264,444 tonnes.
Nickel consumption remained concentrated in stainless steel production, while battery demand provided a more limited contribution. The report also described production constraints in Indonesia, including ore quota restrictions and water shortages that had affected some smelting operations.
Together, the October market data showed differing conditions across the three metals, with copper recording substantial annual price gains, nickel posting a smaller yearly increase despite recent weakness, and cobalt experiencing declines over both monthly and annual periods.
Exploration Programs and Resource Definition Plans at Majuba Hill
Separate from the proposed Labrador acquisition, Copper One outlined drilling activities, exploration targets, and resource-definition objectives at its flagship Majuba Hill copper-silver-gold project in Pershing County, Nevada.
Majuba Hill covers approximately 9,684 acres, or 3,919 hectares, comprising 403 federal lode mining claims and two private parcels. The property is located approximately 70 miles southwest of Winnemucca and 156 miles northeast of Reno, with a power substation approximately 22 miles from the site.
Copper One reported more than 90,000 feet, or 27,127 meters, of drilling across more than 110 holes at Majuba Hill. The company completed multiple drilling phases between 2020 and 2025, including five diamond drill holes totaling 5,484.5 feet, or 1,671.7 meters, during 2025.

articles.title: Gold and copper underpin junior resources outlook as LNG revenues look to rise - Proactive financial news
articles.summary: Gold and copper underpin junior resources outlook as LNG revenues look to rise  Proactive financial news
articles.full_text:
The broader backdrop for Australian junior resources companies remains supportive in several key commodities, with gold continuing to provide one of the strongest macro tailwinds for transactions and project development.
The latest federal Resources and Energy Quarterly forecasts annual Australian gold export earnings of around A$68 billion over the coming years, supporting strategic consolidation and continued interest from larger producers in established exploration and development assets.
Copper also retains a strong structural outlook as electrification, grid investment and data-centre construction lift demand, with Australian copper export earnings forecast to rise from around A$14 billion in 2025-26 to A$19 billion in real terms by 2030-31.
Lithium is expected to stage a near-term recovery, with export earnings forecast to rise from A$10.2 billion to A$17 billion in 2026-27, although expanding global supply continues to present medium-term price risk.
Exploration spending also remains robust, with Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data showing seasonally adjusted mineral exploration expenditure of A$1.143 billion in the June quarter, up 3.9% quarter-on-quarter and 17.9% year-on-year.
The increase points to continuing activity across the exploration sector, while also intensifying competition for drilling capacity, laboratory services and investor capital.
Source: Resources and Energy Quarterly
The energy mix
Australia’s resource and energy export earnings are forecast to rise to about $422 billion in 2026–27 as higher oil and liquefied natural gas prices linked to the Middle East conflict provide a near-term boost.
The Australian Government’s September 2026 Resources and Energy Quarterly said forecasts for 2026–27 and 2027–28 had been revised modestly higher from the June edition, although earnings are expected to decline later in the outlook period as energy prices and export volumes ease.
Export earnings are forecast to increase from $403 billion in 2025–26 to $422 billion in 2026–27 before falling to $391 billion in 2027–28 and easing further to $379 billion by 2030–31, equivalent to $343 billion in real terms.
LNG revenues set to jump
Liquefied natural gas is expected to be a major beneficiary of current market disruption, with tighter shipping conditions in the Middle East intensifying competition among buyers ahead of the northern hemisphere winter.
LNG prices rose above US$25 per million British thermal units in September, while Australian LNG export earnings are forecast to climb from $57 billion in 2025–26 to $70 billion in 2026–27.
The Resources and Energy Quarterly expects LNG prices to decline as Middle East supply conditions normalise and additional US and Qatari supply enters the market, with export values projected to fall to about $42 billion in real terms by 2030–31.
Spot LNG prices are forecast to ease from US$18.30 per million British thermal units in 2026 to around US$8.50 by 2031 in real terms.
Oil prices remain elevated
Oil prices were still above US$100 a barrel at the time of the report, reflecting restricted exports from several major Middle Eastern producers.
Prices are expected to remain elevated in the near term before declining and stabilising at around US$65 a barrel in real terms over the later years of the outlook period.
Australia’s oil export earnings are forecast to fall from $10.9 billion in 2025–26 to $5.6 billion in real terms by 2030–31 as prices and volumes decline.
The report also expects the Middle East conflict to weigh on global economic growth in the short term, although investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, supply-chain resilience and the energy transition is expected to provide support.
World growth is forecast at 2.9% to 3.0% in 2026, rising to 3.4% in 2027 before moderating to around 3.1% to 3.2% over the remainder of the outlook period.

articles.title: Oil Price Forecast: Brent Hits $111.75 Then Falls to $106.85, WTI $96.17 — $102 Target - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Oil Price Forecast: Brent Hits $111.75 Then Falls to $106.85, WTI $96.17 — $102 Target  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Brent fell $4.90 from its $111.75 five-month high to $106.85 as Houthi strike claims went unconfirmed.
- U.S. commercial crude stocks fell 8.6 million barrels to 415.6 million, against a 288,000-barrel forecast.
- OPEC+ holds November quotas at 31.01 million bpd while Gulf exports run at 60% to 80% of normal.
Brent crude for December delivery traded at $106.85 per barrel in the New York afternoon on Tuesday, down $2.70, or 2.46%, from Monday’s settlement of $109.55. West Texas Intermediate for December fell $2.37, or 2.41%, to $96.17 from a $98.54 settlement. The session’s headline number came hours earlier. Brent touched $111.75 in the European morning, its highest since May 20, after Yemen’s Houthi forces claimed strikes on a Saudi Aramco facility at Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and airports in Riyadh and Abha. From that peak, Brent fell $4.90, or 4.4%, by the afternoon.
The thesis for this forecast is simple. The oil market is carrying a geopolitical risk premium on top of physical fundamentals that are tight but not breaking, and Tuesday showed how quickly that premium can drain when the attacks are claimed but not confirmed. Saudi authorities have not confirmed the Houthi claims. No major supply loss has been verified. Meanwhile, Gulf exports have recovered toward 80% of pre-war volumes, Washington has eased some sanctions on Russian energy, and U.S. commercial inventories, while falling, still sit only about 3% below their five-year average. Brent at $111 priced a supply shock. Brent at $106 prices a supply risk.
The intraday path tells the story. Brent climbed 55 cents to $110.10 by 03:19 GMT, extended to $111.05 by 08:10 GMT, and printed the $111.75 high before New York opened. At 6:45 a.m. in New York, December Brent stood at $111.41, up $1.86. By the U.S. afternoon, it had fallen below $107. The expiring November WTI contract was more violent still, jumping as much as $5.94, or 5.7%, to $109.60 in what looked like a short squeeze into expiry, before the curve snapped back.
The two-week context explains why the reversal matters. Brent settled at $100.58 on October 6. The rally from there to Tuesday’s $111.75 peak added 11.1% in ten sessions, fueled by a string of Gulf incidents. At least 18 vessels were reportedly attacked over the past two weeks. Each new headline added to the premium. Tuesday was the first session in which a major escalation headline failed to hold its gains through the U.S. session.
The levels are clear. For Brent, support sits at $105 to $106, then $102.25 and $100. Resistance sits at $110.70, Monday’s high, then $111.75. For December WTI, support is $95, then $92, with resistance at $98.54 and $100.78, the morning indication. Between those lines, oil will be decided by whether the next attack claim comes with confirmed damage.
Yanbu and Shaybah: Why These Two Targets Matter
The Houthis said on Monday they had launched several attacks on Saudi energy, airport and military targets. The list included an Aramco facility at Yanbu on the Red Sea coast, the Shaybah oilfield in the Empty Quarter, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and Abha airport. Saudi Arabia’s cabinet condemned the Houthi attacks on energy infrastructure without addressing Yanbu or Shaybah specifically. Riyadh postponed its flagship investment conference. Aramco shares fell about 1% on Tuesday.
Yanbu is the critical asset. The Red Sea port serves as Saudi Arabia’s fallback export route when the Strait of Hormuz is constrained. Crude reaches Yanbu through the East-West pipeline from the eastern oil fields, bypassing the Gulf entirely. Since the war waged by the United States and Israel against Iran began on February 28, Yanbu has carried a larger share of Saudi exports than usual. A confirmed hit that took Yanbu’s terminals offline would cut one of the few routes that does not run through Hormuz.
Shaybah is a different kind of risk. The field sits deep inside Saudi territory near the border with the United Arab Emirates and produces light crude. A strike there would show that Houthi drones and missiles can reach Saudi production deep inland, not just coastal infrastructure. That raises the vulnerability of the entire Saudi system, which has 10.5 million barrels a day of quota under OPEC+ for November.
The absence of confirmation is why the premium faded. Markets reacted to the claims at face value in Asian and European trading. As the day went on without satellite imagery, company statements or shipping data showing a disruption, traders started to discount the attacks. The oil market has learned this year that Houthi claims often outrun verified damage.
The broader conflict added to the tension. On Monday, a Houthi attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces in Shabwa province killed 58 people and injured more than 200. Those forces began an offensive earlier this month to retake Houthi-held territory. The escalation inside Yemen raises the risk that the Houthis widen their campaign against Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government.
The Strait of Hormuz remains the larger structural risk. Two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in the strait, and Iran’s Revolutionary Guard threatened to target undersea communication cables in the waterway. Tanker insurance premiums have climbed more than 50%. About a fifth of the world’s crude and liquefied natural gas moves through Hormuz in normal times.
Gulf Exports at 60% to 80% of Normal and OPEC+ Stuck Below Quota
The physical market is tighter than it looks on a chart, and OPEC+ is the reason. The group’s seven core members, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman, agreed on October 4 to keep November production targets unchanged at the September level. Combined quotas total 31.01 million barrels per day. The targets are 10.5 million barrels a day for Saudi Arabia, 9.9 million for Russia, 4.4 million for Iraq, 2.7 million for Kuwait, 1.6 million for Kazakhstan, 1.0 million for Algeria and 0.8 million for Oman.
Those quotas are largely on paper. Gulf OPEC+ producers have been pumping well below their targets because of export disruptions from the war on Iran, with exports fluctuating between 60% and 80% of normal levels in recent months. Oil flows from the Middle East were running at around 80% of pre-conflict volumes in early October. OPEC+ raised its targets for six months earlier in 2026 after years of cuts, but most of those increases never reached the market because the barrels could not get out of the Gulf.
The group still holds about 2 million barrels per day of output cuts covering most members. That spare capacity is real but trapped. Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq could produce more if export routes were open. Until Hormuz traffic normalizes, that capacity cannot reach buyers, which is why the market remains tight despite the group’s nominal increases.
The production gap explains the floor under prices. Even with Brent falling $4.90 from its high on Tuesday, it remains above $100. When OPEC+ cannot deliver its quotas, every barrel that does reach the market is more valuable. The tightness comes from logistics rather than from a lack of oil in the ground.
The next decision point is November 1, when the seven core members meet again. The group is also reviewing members’ production capacity to set quotas for 2027, but the war has delayed that review because it has thrown estimates of future production potential into doubt. A decision to resume increases on November 1 would signal confidence that export routes are reopening. A continued pause would confirm that the group sees no relief yet.
Washington’s view of the post-war market is bearish. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has predicted that once the war with Iran ends, the global oil market will face a significant supply surplus, driving prices sharply lower. That view rests on the trapped OPEC+ capacity coming back online at the same time as recovering Gulf exports. For now, it is a forecast about the end of the war, not about October.
Russia Sanctions Waiver Added Barrels the Market Did Not Expect
The second force pulling prices down on Tuesday came from Washington. Traders assessed the impact of a potential waiver on Russian energy after President Trump signed an executive order on Friday exempting some sanctions and tariffs on Russian energy exports. That order sent Brent down 31 cents on Monday to settle at $109.55 even as WTI rose.
The waiver matters because Russia is the second-largest producer in OPEC+, with a November quota of 9.9 million barrels per day. Sanctions and tariffs have constrained Russian exports and forced its crude into discounted channels. Easing those restrictions brings more Russian barrels back into mainstream markets, which adds to global supply at the margin and offsets part of the Gulf disruption.
Russia has also been finding new routes. Russian oil exports via the Arctic route jumped amid the global freight crisis, according to shipping data. With the Strait of Hormuz constrained and tanker insurance up more than 50%, Russian crude shipped from northern ports has filled part of the gap left by Gulf producers. The waiver makes those barrels easier to sell.
The geopolitical picture with Russia is not simple. Ukraine struck Russian oil facilities in recent days, and tensions between Ukraine and the United States have added to uncertainty. Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries and export terminals have been a recurring supply risk throughout 2026. The waiver eases one constraint on Russian exports while the conflict creates another.
The net effect on Tuesday was bearish. The combination of an unconfirmed Houthi strike and a confirmed U.S. policy that adds Russian supply tipped the balance. The market priced the policy change more heavily than the attack claim once U.S. traders were at their desks.

articles.title: When mining becomes strategic: are critical minerals testing investor-state arbitration? - Stewarts Law
articles.summary: When mining becomes strategic: are critical minerals testing investor-state arbitration?  Stewarts Law
articles.full_text:
As critical minerals become geopolitically strategic, resulting disputes become political. Investor-state (or investment treaty) arbitration is a common forum for such disputes. Daniel Wilmot, International Arbitration partner at Stewarts asks: Does this present a challenge for such arbitration? If so, how should it acknowledge such reality?
Across Africa, a “new wave” of mining disputes is emerging. A recent data-led analysis by Stewarts, a disputes-only law firm, identified 43 publicly reported mining-related investor-state arbitrations brought or contemplated against African states between 1 January 2020 and 24 June 2026.
The disputes analysed concerned bauxite, graphite, uranium, lithium, cobalt, copper, and gold. Many arose from measures affecting mining rights, including revoking or suspending licences, changing regulatory frameworks, refusing to extend or implement operating arrangements, and removing control over mining assets.
Although that analysis was subject to the methodology and limitations described, it nonetheless points to a trend. One resulting question may be whether such a trend is limited to a mere increase in case numbers, or whether it reflects a change in the environment in which mining disputes are arising. As states increasingly regard certain mineral resources as strategically important, what impact is that having on dispute resolution?
And if there is an impact, how should a three-person tribunal in closed-door arbitration proceedings address political considerations without allowing them to determine its decisions?
From private concessions to strategically important assets
Critical minerals are not a single, fixed category. What makes a mineral critical depends on a number of factors: availability, its application, the concentration and security of its supply and (as illustrated by the events in the Strait of Hormuz) the consequences of disruption.
Lithium, cobalt, nickel, and graphite are important to battery production. Rare earth elements have applications across advanced manufacturing and digital technology. Uranium, of course, remains significant to nuclear-energy supply. The result is that a mine producing these resources may no longer be regarded simply as a privately operated commercial asset. Such assets will increasingly form part of a state’s industrial strategy, energy policy, and geopolitical value and bargaining. As the International Energy Agency (IEA) put it in its Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 report, “critical minerals have rapidly moved to the heart of global discussions on energy and economic security”.
Africa plays a central role in this evolution. The continent possesses substantial deposits required by an increasingly mineral-hungry world. Yet, it is said it captures only a limited share of their economic value: extracting and exporting raw minerals often produces far less domestic value than the processing, manufacturing, industries, and technologies they support.
It is understandable that African states should thus seek a greater participation in their mining sectors. This may take the form of increased royalties or state ownership, domestic-processing requirements, revised fiscal arrangements, export restrictions or, at its extreme, the forced reallocation of mining rights altogether.
This shift is often coined “resource nationalism”: linguistically accurate but a label that may obscure legitimate development questions. states must manage natural resources in their people’s interests and ensure their development produces meaningful economic benefit.
A legitimate political objective does not automatically validate the means of pursuing it, however. Mining rights will remain governed by contractual commitments, domestic legislation and regulation, and international treaties guaranteeing certain investor rights.
Here the tension arises. Investors should expect regulation to evolve over time, especially during long-term mining projects, but will still also expect the protections treaties seek to guarantee, ie, that state decisions be consistent, fair, equal, and transparent.
Disputes often arise where those expectations meet.
The ‘wave’ of such disputes on the continent
As the same IEA report notes, countries are introducing measures to protect and preserve their mineral interests. To point to a few examples, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has introduced a cobalt export quota. Zimbabwe and Mozambique have imposed trade restrictions on lithium and graphite, respectively. The IEA cites the DRC quota policy as a real example of global supply risk.
This context perhaps explains the perceived increase (or wave) in mining-related disputes across the continent. The earlier Stewarts analysis identified, for example, five mining-related arbitrations involving Guinea, all brought in 2025 or 2026, following a five-year period in which no such case had been identified. Four cases were identified involving Niger, all brought in 2024 or 2025, while two cases concerning Burundi were brought in 2026. Further disputes involving Mali and the DRC arose at different points between 2020 and 2026.
Alongside the growth in numbers, the cases also revealed a degree of consistency in the measures giving rise to the claims. Those measures principally affected the ownership, control, or continued validity of mining rights. And that pattern appears to remain current. Of the 17 cases comprising the relevant part of the dataset, 13 were recorded as pending in early September 2026. One of the most recent, Falcon Energy Materials PLC v Republic of Guinea, was commenced on 16 March 2026 and registered by the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) on 31 March 2026 . In that case, the claimant investor alleges that Guinea unlawfully revoked the exploitation licence for the Lola graphite project and seeks compensation under the 2011 United Arab Emirates-Guinea bilateral investment treaty.
These developments do not establish that all mining disputes are becoming political or that every state measure affecting a mining project reflects a coordinated strategy. The wider dataset reviewed by Stewarts includes conventional contractual, fiscal, and ownership disputes that cannot properly be attributed to “resource nationalism” in the sense described.
The dataset nevertheless indicates a potential structural shift in both how and why a growing number of disputes are arising in the mining and minerals space across Africa.
Public interest versus legal entitlement
If that is right, the political imperatives underlying the sources of some of these disputes are being assessed by tribunals constituted in the investment treaty arbitrations charged with resolving them. This means such tribunals will face defences justified by reference to domestic value creation, environmental protection, national security, supply chain resilience, local community stakeholder interests or, more generally, the need to correct a perceived unequal allocation of the economic benefits flowing from the use of such minerals.
Tribunals will be pressed to take these points seriously. And the due process nature of arbitration is such that tribunals may well be required positively to engage with them. So tribunals cannot ignore such considerations, especially where they are relevant to the applicable legal standards under treaties. But, equally, they cannot be treated as a substitute for legal analysis. The political (or econo-ethical) cart must not be put before the legal horse.
How might such public interest points be best understood in an arbitral context? Perhaps as part of the factual and regulatory context in which legal rights operate. It might inform the assessment of an investor’s legitimate expectations, the character and purpose of a state measure, whether treatment was arbitrary or discriminatory, and whether the measure bore a rational or proportionate relationship to its stated objective. It might also affect analyses of causation, contributory conduct, and damages. But, absent express treaty wording, care should be taken to avoid it becoming a free-standing basis on which legal rights are displaced.
The principles are perhaps clearer. The strategic importance of a mineral does not give a state an unrestricted licence to disregard contractual or treaty obligations. Equally, investment treaty protection does not guarantee that the legal and regulatory environment will remain unchanged throughout the decades-long life of a mining project. Although such principles are easy to state, it may well prove harder to apply them in practice in a dispute.
Transparent reasoning in awards therefore assumes particular importance. Tribunals should identify why wider context is legally relevant, the weight attached to it, and how legitimate regulation is distinguished from compensable wrongdoing. Each case turns on its merits, but such discipline should allow arbitration to recognise political and developmental realities without becoming political in itself.
It is not just the reasoning; it is who formulates it
If transparent reasoning gains greater importance in the context of such politically infused cases, so does the identity of those formulating it. This changing dispute landscape has implications for tribunal constitution, particularly because tribunals are partly party-appointed.
It is an oft-commented perception that some arbitrators in investment treaty arbitrations are known to be investor- or state-friendly. Critical-minerals cases should not require ‘political’ arbitrators, or those selected for presumed sympathy with state sovereignty or investor protection. They require tribunals able to distinguish political assertion from legally relevant context and understand the technical and economic evidence on which that distinction depends. Tribunal expertise is therefore likely to be a key consideration in its selection.

On October 15, 2026, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) took two related steps to streamline natural gas infrastructure permitting under sections 3 and 7 of the Natural Gas Act (NGA). First, it issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NOPR) on Authorizations for Certain Activities at Liquefied Natural Gas Plants. The NOPR (Docket No. RM26-2-001), if finalized, would amend regulations implementing sections 3 and 7 of the NGA to create a three-tiered blanket authorization program for FERC-regulated liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities. The proposals are intended to build on the record developed through FERC’s November 2025 Notice of Inquiry, which examined expedited approvals of certain routine replacements, upgrades and modest expansions of LNG terminals without the need for case-specific reviews and approvals.
Second, FERC published a Draft Policy Statement on Efficient Environmental Reviews of Natural Gas Project Applications. The Draft Policy Statement (Docket No. PL26-3-000) would separately end FERC’s routine requirement for operational air dispersion modeling from applicants seeking approval under NGA sections 3 and 7 for LNG facilities and pipeline compressor station projects, while retaining emissions disclosure, Clean Air Act (CAA) compliance, and project-specific environmental review. These models have been used by FERC to assess the “significance” of these projects’ air impacts on their immediate vicinity under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). FERC’s rationale for the Draft Policy Statement leans heavily on NEPA reforms in the 2023 BUILDER Act, discussed here, and the Supreme Court’s 2025 Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado (Seven County) decision, explained here. In an emphasis on the need to simplify its NEPA process, FERC distinguished its use of the models from those of environmental regulatory agencies that make substantive decisions about air emissions under the CAA. FERC continued to emphasize the need for CAA compliance while removing the models from its own critical path for NEPA compliance.
Key Gas Infrastructure Permitting Changes Proposed by FERC
Proposed LNG Plant Blanket Authorization Program
While FERC has been regulating LNG facilities for decades, until now it has never sought to create a blanket authorization or prior notice program for those facilities. It has maintained a case-specific program, both for the initial project permit, and to approve any future modifications, all subject to Parts 153 and 157 of its regulations. When FERC initiated a blanket review program for pipelines in the 1980s under section 7 of the NGA, it declined to extend it to LNG plant facilities on grounds that they were not “routine” and required more case-specific engineering, environmental and safety reviews. FERC reiterated this position in 2006.
The NOPR reverses course, announcing that since 2006, FERC has reviewed over 100 applications related to LNG facilities, generating a sufficient body of experience to quell its prior concerns. FERC acknowledges that its current case-by-case review process can be administratively inefficient and burdensome, especially for certain replacements, modifications and small expansions. To expedite and simplify the regulatory process, FERC proposes a three-tier system of Automatic Authorization projects, 60-day prior notice projects and 90-day prior notice projects depending on the scope of work required:
| Tier | Eligible Activities | Key Conditions | 
| Automatic authorization | Replacements, modifications and additions that do not increase authorized capacity, stay within the authorized footprint and design limits, and have no adverse safety or reliability impacts | Only minor or no environmental effects; reported in semi-annual operational reports; no notice to proceed required | 
| 60-day prior notice | Modifications designed to increase authorized capacity that remain within the footprint and design limits; related section 3 pipeline facilities to the extent allowed under the Part 157 program | Public notice and protest; U.S. Department of Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Administration (PHMSA) Letter of Determination, U.S. Coast Guard (USCG) Letter of Recommendation, Department of War (DoW) concurrence and state safety coordination as applicable | 
| 90-day prior notice | New LNG facilities and auxiliary systems (e.g., liquefaction trains, tanks, marine berths) outside the authorized footprint | No more than 25 acres permanently occupied on adjacent, previously disturbed or developed land in industrial or unzoned areas; same facility type as previously authorized; anti-segmentation rule | 
The proposal would also require notice to affected landowners and municipalities at least 45 days before most automatic-authorization construction, subject to specified exceptions, and generally within three business days from assignment of a docket number for a prior-notice request.
The proposals are modeled on the existing automatic authorization and prior notice rules for pipelines under Part 157 of FERC’s regulations, with certain key differences.
Notably, there are no cost thresholds or caps for project eligibility.
FERC does not deem costs to be an appropriate proxy for environmental or operational impacts in the LNG context.
And, unless the facilities are rate regulated under NGA section 7, costs also are irrelevant.
All larger LNG import and export terminals are subject only to NGA section 3, without regulated rates.
FERC also proposes longer periods for projects to enter service.
Whereas the pipeline program requires prior notice projects to be placed in service within one year, the NOPR proposes to give LNG projects five years to complete construction and enter service.
In addition, while pipeline projects are subject to a two-tier program of blanket authorization and 60-day prior notice projects, the LNG program would add a third tier, recognizing that certain LNG projects require additional review time but could nonetheless proceed without a case-specific authorization.
Another difference concerns notices to proceed with construction and operation.
The pipeline program requires no notice to proceed once the prior notice period has ended, allowing construction and operation to begin without further FERC approval.
By contrast, citing FERC’s safety oversight of LNG facilities, the LNG program would require a notice to proceed from the Office of Energy Projects before commissioning or the introduction of hazardous fluids, and again before the commencement of service.
As under the pipeline program, a protest could convert a prior notice project to case-specific review, with FERC retaining the right to dismiss protests that fail to raise a substantive issue.
The NOPR seeks comment on whether protestor eligibility criteria should be narrower and on the target timeline for resolving protests.
Parallel reforms to the pipeline prior notice program are under review in Docket No.
RM25-12 in a NOPR initiated earlier this year.

In order to be eligible for the blanket authorization program, holders of case-specific authorizations will need to apply to FERC, as opposed to being grandfathered into the program as industry commenters had urged. There also are additional changes for LNG plants holding NGA section 7 certificates. These facilities also would be eligible for receipt of a blanket authorization. Two years after the Final Rule’s effective date, these plants would lose access to their section 2.55 auxiliary and replacement authority, which was deemed superfluous in the event a blanket authorization is received.
The NOPR does not propose to create a new categorical exclusion under FERC’s NEPA implementation regulations for Blanket Authorization or Prior Notice LNG projects. Instead, it proposes that FERC will prepare a programmatic environmental impact statement for Blanket Authorization projects while Prior Notice projects will be permitted to argue why they are subject to an existing categorical exclusion, or provide sufficient information for FERC to perform an environmental assessment (EA). FERC currently prepares environmental assessments for certain pipeline prior notice projects within a 60-day period, and may need to prepare similar documents for LNG facilities in similarly tight timeframes.
Commissioner Judy Chang (D) issued a concurrence supporting the program but questioning the 90-day prior notice 25-acre limit proposal, noting that an additional 25 acres could accommodate an additional liquefaction train. She asks whether applicants should be required to affirmatively demonstrate no significant impact for previously unstudied areas and whether FERC should cap the number of expansions or set a minimum interval between them.
Proposed Draft Policy Statement
The Draft Policy Statement is framed as a way of rebalancing FERC’s NEPA review obligations in light of its statutory purpose as an economic regulator, and following directives from the Supreme Court in Seven County.
Under FERC’s current practice, applicants for LNG facility authorizations under NGA section 3 and for compressor station certificates of public convenience and necessity under NGA section 7 are instructed to follow FERC’s 2017 Guidance Manual for Environmental Report Preparation (Guidance Manual), which includes the preparation of a screening or refined air dispersion model, providing comparisons to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). articles.summary: The Government Can Set the Price of Rare Earths. It Cannot Set Their Value.  InvestorNews
articles.full_text:
In a Financial Times commentary published on October 8, 2026, economist Mohamed El-Erian examines the United States Treasury’s growing willingness to intervene directly in financial markets to achieve political and economic objectives. He cites the Argentine peso, American Treasury bond yields, and the Japanese yen. His underlying argument is that government intervention can succeed when it aligns with economic fundamentals, but can fail, sometimes spectacularly, when political objectives replace those fundamentals. I believe El-Erian’s analysis applies directly to the current American effort to rebuild a domestic critical minerals industry, particularly the attempt to establish a non-Chinese rare earth supply chain. Indeed, I think the consequences of government intervention in critical minerals pricing may ultimately matter more for American manufacturing than the financial market interventions he discusses.
The United States government has entered a new era of economic statecraft in which national security considerations increasingly determine capital allocation. The federal government is no longer content simply to regulate, tax, subsidize, or purchase industrial products. It is becoming an investor, a lender, a price guarantor, and, in some cases, a preferred customer. It also tries to decide which industries should exist in the United States, how quickly they should develop, and what prices their products should command. The difficulty is that governments can create financial incentives, but they cannot repeal the laws of chemistry, physics, engineering, or economics. For the critical minerals industry, this distinction is fundamental, and I fear that Washington’s current enthusiasm for industrial intervention is obscuring it.
I have argued for years that the American discussion of critical minerals reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of the industrial supply chain. A mineral deposit is not a metal, a metal is not necessarily an industrial material, and an industrial material is not a qualified component ready for use by an original equipment manufacturer. The economic value of a mineral deposit is determined not simply by the quantity of an element that it contains, but by the cost of extracting that element, separating it from the other constituents of the deposit, converting it into a useful chemical or metallic form, and ultimately manufacturing a product that a customer can and will purchase. A rare earth deposit may contain substantial quantities of neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium, but unless those elements can be economically recovered, separated, refined, converted into metals and alloys, and incorporated into qualified magnets, the deposit’s theoretical value may have little relationship to its commercial value.
The American government appears increasingly determined to accelerate this process through financial intervention. Its objective is understandable. China dominates the commercial production and processing of rare earths and has developed an industrial infrastructure that the United States allowed to disappear over several decades. But losing that infrastructure was not simply a financial event. It was an industrial and technological event, involving the disappearance of manufacturing capacity, experienced personnel, specialized equipment, customer relationships, and accumulated operating knowledge. Reversing it requires much more than raising raw material prices or subsidizing the market capitalization of companies that claim they intend to restore what was lost.
The clearest example of government intervention in the American rare earth market is the Department of Defense’s July 2025 agreement with MP Materials Corp. (NYSE: MP). Its price protection agreement establishes a ten-year mechanism based on US$110 per NdPr kilogram equivalent, as defined in the contract, covering eligible neodymium-praseodymium in concentrate, oxide, and metal products. Quarterly government payments compensate MP Materials for the shortfall when the contractual volume-weighted benchmark falls below that threshold, subject to the agreement’s eligibility and calculation provisions. After the specified production milestone associated with the 10X facility, the government is entitled to 30% of the amount by which that quarterly benchmark exceeds US$110 per NdPr kilogram equivalent, applied to eligible volumes. This is not an ordinary commercial supply agreement. It explicitly intervenes in the economics of rare earth production, intended to provide revenue certainty for a strategically important domestic producer.
It is important to distinguish this price floor from a universal American market price. The government has not ordered every American buyer to pay US$110 per NdPr kilogram equivalent. Instead, it has established a contractual financial guarantee for a particular producer, based on a specified benchmark. Nevertheless, the agreement has created a powerful reference point for investors, financiers, and other rare earth companies seeking government support. The government is effectively declaring that the prevailing international price may be inadequate to sustain the domestic industrial capacity it considers essential for national security. That judgment may be correct, but acknowledging its possible validity does not mean the US$110 contractual threshold is the economically correct price for every NdPr product, or that every proposed American rare earth project becomes commercially viable at that price.
China’s rare earth industry did not achieve its dominant position through an ideal free market. It benefited from decades of industrial policy, state directed investment, infrastructure development, technological accumulation, and the concentration of manufacturing demand within China. The resulting prices cannot automatically be treated as those that would prevail in a genuinely competitive global market. The United States can therefore reasonably question whether Chinese quotations adequately reflect the cost of creating and maintaining an independent supply chain. But the appropriate question is not whether the American government can establish a price floor. Clearly it can. The question is whether that floor supports a competitive industry or merely shields selected companies from the consequences of their own operating costs.
Unlike copper, aluminum, or gold, the rare earths are not traded in a deep, liquid, transparent international market with universally accepted exchange prices. China has domestic quotations, export quotations, prices reported by specialist agencies, negotiated contract prices, and increasingly government supported Western pricing arrangements. These are not necessarily interchangeable. A kilogram of dysprosium oxide offered in China is not economically identical to a kilogram of qualified dysprosium metal delivered under a long term contract to an American alloy manufacturer. The difference includes processing costs, logistics, financing, specifications, supply security, and the risk that a shipment may not be licensed for export. Consequently, it is entirely reasonable that an American manufacturer might pay a premium for a dependable non-Chinese supply, but that premium must be understood and justified.
Is the buyer paying for an actual improvement in reliability, quality, and delivery security, or is the buyer being asked to subsidize an inefficient production system that cannot otherwise survive? These are very different propositions. The first represents the commercial value of supply chain security, while the second represents a transfer of wealth from the customer or taxpayer to the producer. The distinction becomes particularly important when governments begin treating prices in their own financial support agreements as evidence of an entire industry’s market value. A government guaranteed price is not proof of an independently sustainable commercial market, and a price established for national security reasons should never be confused with a price discovered through competitive commercial transactions.
I believe that the world is moving toward two increasingly distinct rare earth pricing systems. The first is the China centered industrial market, where the overwhelming concentration of separation, metal making, alloy production, and magnet manufacturing gives China enormous influence over prices and availability. The second is an emerging Western strategic market, where governments and manufacturers will pay premiums for materials produced outside Chinese control. These two markets are not inherently irrational. A secure supply has an economic value that may not be reflected in the lowest available spot quotation. The danger arises when the strategic premium detaches from the actual cost and performance of the alternative supply chain, creating an artificial pricing structure that encourages investment in capacity without showing the capacity can operate competitively.
In a hypothetical example, consider an American producer that requires US$110 per kilogram for a specified NdPr product to cover its costs, while a competing Chinese producer can deliver the same specification on comparable terms for US$70. The illustrative US$40 difference might represent the legitimate cost of maintaining a strategically independent source. It might also represent poor recovery rates, inefficient processing, excessive capital expenditure, inadequate plant utilization, or an uncompetitive business model. The price difference alone cannot tell us which explanation is correct. That requires industrial due diligence, not political enthusiasm. The same question matters even more for dysprosium and terbium, where limited non-Chinese separation capacity, restricted export availability, and relatively small market volumes can drive enormous price volatility. articles.title: Uzbekistan, ReElement agree on critical minerals pilot - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Uzbekistan, ReElement agree on critical minerals pilot  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Uzbekistan and U.S.-based ReElement Technologies agreed to develop and launch a joint pilot project for advanced critical minerals processing, Uzbek Investment, Industry and Trade Minister Laziz Kudratov said following a meeting with company Director Mark LaVerghetta in Samarkand on October 19.
This was reflected in the statement by Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.
The discussions focused on opportunities to process critical minerals using advanced technologies and introduce modern processing solutions in Uzbekistan, according to the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.
Additionally, the sides explored potential joint investment initiatives involving technological solutions for the critical minerals sector. The agreement to develop and launch a pilot project followed the meeting, although the parties did not disclose its scope, investment value, location or implementation timeline.
ReElement Technologies is a U.S.-based critical minerals refining company headquartered in Fishers, Indiana. It specializes in separating and purifying rare earth elements and critical battery materials using chromatography-based technology, which can process both mined resources and recycled materials.
The company's technology is designed to recover and refine materials such as rare earth elements, lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese for use in magnets, batteries and other industrial applications. Its modular processing systems can be deployed at mining or manufacturing sites and scaled to meet production requirements.
ReElement is a subsidiary of American Resources Corporation, a U.S. company focused on critical mineral supply chains and natural resource development.

articles.title: American Rare Earths Is Betting That Scale Is the Easy Part - InvestorNews
articles.summary: American Rare Earths Is Betting That Scale Is the Easy Part  InvestorNews
articles.full_text:
At Halleck Creek, Mark Wall’s priority is turning a vast Wyoming rare earth resource into a commercially viable American supply chain. In a recent conversation with Tracy Hughes, the Chief Executive Officer of American Rare Earths Limited (ASX: ARR | OTCQX: ARRNF | ADR: AMRRY) explained why growing the deposit is no longer the company’s immediate focus. That shift is the most interesting thing about American Rare Earths right now, and it frames both the opportunity and the risk.
The headline numbers come from the updated Scoping Study for the Cowboy State Mine, the initial development phase of Halleck Creek in Wyoming. It estimates an after-tax net present value of approximately US$1.07 billion at an 8% real discount rate and an after-tax internal rate of return of 21%. Initial capital is estimated at approximately US$900 million, including contingency, and the model assumes an NdPr oxide price of US$151 per kilogram. These are preliminary project economics, with no ore reserves declared, rather than an established valuation of the company or a completed mine-to-magnet business.
Wall’s gloss on the scale is the telling part. The initial mine plan “uses around 4% of the resource, which really just gives a sense of scale of this deposit.” The broader Halleck Creek mineral resource stands at approximately 2.63 billion tonnes, grading 3,292 parts per million total rare earth oxides. The distinction matters: the initial mine plan uses a small fraction of Halleck Creek, while the Cowboy State Mine resource itself represents a substantially larger share of the overall deposit.
That is why the latest drilling focused on improving geological confidence and supporting development studies. Infill drilling can support future reserve estimation, but declaring reserves also requires the relevant technical and economic assessments. Wall described the mineralization as “porphyry-like”, contiguous and consistent, and said the campaign also tested theories about where grade runs a little higher. In a bulk, low-grade system, modest grade gains in the early years can matter disproportionately to payback. That detail deserves more attention than the drill metres.
The harder question is whether the company can help carry the project from rock through to the magnet supply chain. Wall is explicit that this is the ambition. “This is a technology business,” he said. “We’re trying to get through to the end product, which is a magnet, which essentially enables technology to move.” The upstream, he concedes, is “a fairly simple mine.” The difficulty, and much of the potential value, lies downstream in processing, separation and metallization, where commercial execution remains to be demonstrated.
The pilot program is therefore the thing to watch. At the time of the interview, Wall said material had been mined and crushed in Wyoming and that the concentration circuit was awaiting a final equipment item. The company’s published program envisages concentration work in Wyoming followed by hydrometallurgical processing at Saskatchewan Research Council, with separated rare earth oxide targeted for late Q2 2027. Wall says hydrometallurgical recoveries are already very good and identifies physical separation as the place “where we see real opportunity to improve further the economics of the project by increasing the recoveries.” That identifies beneficiation as an important area for improvement, while the financial case also remains sensitive to product prices and costs.
The midstream runs through an August 2026 memorandum of understanding with Novex, LLC. It covers oxide-to-metal test work and collaboration on the design of a domestic metal production facility to be built by American Rare Earths, with a definitive long-term agreement targeted within 12 months. Wall expects progress over the coming months, but commercial production and final arrangements remain ahead. Partnering can reduce the need to develop every technology internally; it also makes the terms of those relationships important to future control and margins.
Then there is the listing question. American Rare Earths trades in Sydney and on the U.S. OTC market, while Halleck Creek is held through its wholly owned subsidiary, Wyoming Rare (USA) Inc. The company is preparing for a proposed additional Nasdaq listing, with ASX expected to remain the primary listing. Its JORC Scoping Study shares its technical basis with a parallel SEC S-K 1300 Initial Assessment. “I think a vertically integrated company is going to receive more recognition on the U.S. exchange than it currently does on the Australian exchange,” Wall said. Broader investor access could help its cost of capital, but any valuation benefit still depends on the project’s technical and commercial progress.
Executing that project requires people with operating experience. Wall’s background includes Placer Dome, Western Mining Corporation and Barrick, where he served as Senior Vice President & Operations Officer. Director Matthew Gili, President and CEO of Casper-based Ur-Energy Inc., was Chief Operating Officer of Oyu Tolgoi, Managing Director of Palabora Mining Company and Chief Technical Officer at Barrick, according to his official biography. Chief Commercial Officer Nick Lissolo brings 17 years of mining finance, project evaluation and capital allocation experience, including senior roles at Newmont. Hughes noted that the company was adding “a sophisticated professional engineer” to its board rather than “another billionaire.” The observation points to the practical demands of moving a project toward construction.
Wall also leans hard on jurisdiction. Wyoming offers regional rail, highway and power infrastructure, alongside an established mining and energy industry. The state ranked fourth globally in the Fraser Institute’s 2024 Investment Attractiveness Index, although it was excluded from the 2025 rankings because of insufficient survey responses. Having worked across several continents, Wall insists infrastructure “is so, so important, especially in this business.” For a bulk-tonnage operation, access to transport and power is central to the economics, although project-specific infrastructure requirements still need to be resolved.
Asked what shareholders should look for over the next quarter, Wall offered something unusually modest: “stability of execution.” He added that the team will “continue to say what we’re going to do and then do that.” The useful measures are progress in recovery testing, metallization work with Novex, Nasdaq preparations and the geological and engineering studies needed to advance the project. His promise of “lots to follow in the next three to six months” should be read as an expectation of updates, rather than a timetable for completing all those workstreams.
The Western drive to establish alternative rare earth supply chains gives American Rare Earths a supportive backdrop. Converting that interest into funding and a commercially proven operation remains the company’s task. The test is whether an experienced team can turn an enormous resource into consistent, qualified industrial products at a cost customers will support. Size, as Wall keeps reminding us, is no longer the immediate question.

articles.full_text:
Recently, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) held its October press conference. Ren Zhongbao, Deputy Director of the Department of Innovation and High-Tech Development of the NDRC, responded to a media question on how the principle of "adapting measures to local conditions" in the Opinions on Developing New Quality Productive Forces will be implemented. He stated that the essence of adapting measures to local conditions is seeking truth from facts, and this principle must be applied throughout the entire process of developing new quality productive forces.
Planning and Layout Must Be Scientific and Rational to Avoid a Rush of Undisciplined Action
Ren Zhongbao pointed out that China has a vast territory, with significant differences in resource endowments, industrial foundations, scientific and educational resources, and innovation capabilities across regions. Therefore, the primary directions for developing new quality productive forces should naturally differ from place to place. When planning and laying out key industrial sectors for development and proposing major projects, each region must fully assess whether it possesses the corresponding foundational conditions, and resolutely avoid a rush of undisciplined action and indiscriminate expansion. The NDRC will, in accordance with relevant national regulations, ensure the alignment of special plans for future industries and emerging pillar industries at the national and provincial levels, strengthen the provincial development and reform departments' control over and alignment with the formulation of special plans at the city and county levels, and guide all regions to identify development tracks suited to their actual conditions while adhering to the principle of national coordination.
Project Arrangements Should Leverage Comparative Advantages; A Plan for Hydrogen Energy Investment Layout Is Being Formulated
The Opinions explicitly state that "serious accountability shall be pursued for major losses caused by a rush of undisciplined action and blind investment." Ren Zhongbao said that both national and local authorities must conduct in-depth assessments when organizing projects to avoid blind investment and wasteful spending.For example, in response to the recent overheating of investment in certain segments of hydrogen energy, we are formulating a plan that takes into account national strategic needs, technological maturity, and factor support conditions. This plan will rationally lay out major projects and guide local authorities to identify their own positioning and achieve differentiated development in tackling key core technologies, demonstrating renewable energy-based hydrogen production, and expanding application scenarios.
Support Policies Should Be Standardized and Precise, Not a "One-Size-Fits-All Model"
The Opinions explicitly state that "the misuse of policies in the name of developing new quality productive forces is strictly prohibited," which is a bottom line that must be upheld. Ren Zhongbao emphasized that local authorities must be urged to use policies in accordance with laws and regulations, in line with the requirements for building a unified national market, and must not cross the policy red lines drawn for comprehensively addressing "involution-style" competition and rectifying predatory investment promotion. At the same time, a "one-size-fits-all model" should not be adopted. Greater emphasis should be placed on targeted support, such as supporting international science and technology innovation centers and regional innovation centers in enhancing their independent innovation capabilities and cultivating new development tracks, and supporting the northeastern and central regions in using digital intelligence technologies and green technologies to drive industrial transformation and upgrading and climb toward the high end of the industry chain.
The NDRC's clear intention to formulate a layout plan to address the overheating of investment in certain segments of hydrogen energy will help guide rational investment and differentiated development in the hydrogen energy industry, avoid homogeneous competition and low-level redundant construction, and promote the high-quality development of the hydrogen energy industry.

articles.title: Glencore clears key hurdle for Peru copper expansion - Mining.com
articles.summary: Glencore clears key hurdle for Peru copper expansion  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Glencore (LON: GLEN) has secured the land access agreements needed to advance its Coroccohuayco copper expansion in southern Peru, clearing a major hurdle for a project expected to extend the life of its Antapaccay mining complex to more than 40 years.
The Swiss commodities giant said its Peruvian subsidiary, Compañía Minera Antapaccay, completed agreements covering the remaining land parcels required for the brownfield project in Espinar, Cusco. The company is now pursuing final permits, with first production targeted for the second half of 2029.
“Securing access to the required land is an important milestone for Coroccohuayco and for the long-term future of the wider Antapaccay operation, and complements the MEIA environmental approval received earlier in the year,” Luis Rivera, Glencore’s chief operating officer for South America, said in a statement.
The development forms part of Glencore’s broader push to expand its copper business as it pursues a long-term goal of nearly doubling global output. Peru is central to that strategy, although lengthy permitting processes and recurring tensions between mining companies and local communities remain obstacles to bringing new production online.
Longer mine life
Coroccohuayco is expected to increase Antapaccay’s copper production while extending operations at one of the Cusco region’s established mining centres. The existing mine began production in 2012 and produced about 146,000 tonnes of copper last year.
The expansion could also sustain employment, local procurement and economic activity in Espinar for decades, according to Jon Evans, Glencore’s industrial lead for copper.
The company has pledged to continue working with local communities and authorities as the development moves through its remaining regulatory requirements.
Peru’s mining sector has faced persistent challenges involving environmental concerns, community opposition and bureaucratic delays. Major copper developments can take decades to progress from exploration to production, raising costs and complicating investment decisions.
These risks remain relevant to Coroccohuayco despite its environmental approval and newly secured land access. The project must still obtain the remaining permits before construction and production can proceed as planned.
Regional copper ambitions
Glencore has also strengthened its position around Antapaccay through its acquisition of the nearby Quechua copper project, previously held by Pan Pacific Copper.
Quechua, which remained undeveloped under its former owner, adds another potential source of future production to a district that includes the operating Antapaccay mine and the planned Coroccohuayco expansion.
The acquisition could create opportunities for infrastructure sharing and operational efficiencies across Glencore’s holdings, although the company has not outlined a development timetable for Quechua.
Beyond its wholly controlled operations, Glencore holds a 34% interest in Peru’s Antamina copper and zinc mine alongside BHP (ASX: BHP; NYSE: BHP), Teck Resources (TSX: TECK.B)(NYSE: TECK) and Mitsubishi Corp. (TYO: 8058).
Together, the investments give Glencore a substantial position in one of the world’s leading copper-producing countries as miners seek additional supply to meet demand from electrification, power infrastructure and industrial growth.

articles.title: Copper surplus masks looming $332B mine shortfall - Mining.com
articles.summary: Copper surplus masks looming $332B mine shortfall  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
The copper industry needs $332 billion in new mine investment to avert a supply shortage that could begin in 2028, even as refined metal production is expected to outpace demand over the next two years.
Global copper consumption is forecast to rise 61% between 2026 and 2050 to nearly 46 million tonnes, leaving a potential deficit of 20 million tonnes, or 44% of projected demand, according to BloombergNEF’s Transition Metals Outlook 2026, released Tuesday.
The forecast contrasts with the International Copper Study Group’s (ICSG) near-term outlook, which projects a refined copper surplus of 368,000 tonnes in 2027, up from 104,000 tonnes in 2026.
The difference reflects two measures of supply. ICSG tracks refined copper production against consumption, while BloombergNEF (BNEF) examines whether mining capacity can satisfy demand over the coming decades. Higher smelter output could keep refined metal available in the near term without addressing the shortage of new mines needed to support electrification.
Mining investment gap
BNEF expects copper supply to fall short of demand beginning in 2028, with the deficit widening to 3 million tonnes, or 8% of consumption, by 2035. The gap is projected to reach 20 million tonnes, or 44%, by 2050.
Demand is forecast to grow 34% by 2035, driven by copper’s widespread use in vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, electrical wiring and data centres. Its role in clean energy technologies is expected to accelerate consumption as electrification expands.
Supply faces two major constraints: declining ore grades, which make copper increasingly difficult and expensive to extract from existing mines, and insufficient investment in exploration to identify new deposits.
BNEF estimates that new copper mines take an average of 17 years to reach production. Lengthy permitting processes, substantial capital requirements and technical challenges further complicate efforts to expand output before shortages intensify.
Electrified transport is expected to become a major source of demand growth, with copper consumption in the sector forecast to surge 244% to 11.4 million tonnes by 2050 as electric vehicle adoption and supporting infrastructure expand.
Copper stands apart from the other nine materials examined in BNEF’s outlook. The research firm expects lithium, graphite, cobalt, aluminium, nickel, manganese, steel, platinum and palladium to have sufficient long-term production capacity to support electrification through 2050.
That distinction makes copper a potentially greater obstacle to the energy transition than several battery materials that have attracted substantial investment in recent years.
Processing concentration
The outlook also identifies supply chain vulnerabilities beyond mining, particularly the concentration of mineral refining capacity.
Eight of the 10 materials studied have more than half their global refining capacity concentrated in a single country. China holds that dominant position in seven, leaving supply chains exposed to trade restrictions, geopolitical tensions and shifts in industrial policy.
The findings highlight a separate challenge for governments seeking to diversify critical mineral supplies. Expanding mine production alone will not establish independent processing networks, which require additional capital, infrastructure and industrial capacity.
The anticipated refined copper surplus could limit immediate pressure on the market. Stronger smelter production may provide a temporary cushion, although it cannot create additional mined supply.
The industry’s ability to secure financing, permits and construction capacity in the coming years will help determine how severely copper shortages constrain electrification in the 2030s and beyond.

The global cresol-derived frothers market is entering a phase of steady expansion, with demand projected to advance at a compound annual growth rate of 4.2% between 2026 and 2035. Asia-Pacific dominates consumption, representing approximately 55–60% of world demand, as metals refining capacity for electronics-grade copper, lithium, and rare earths continues to expand across China, India, and Southeast Asia. The market is also shaped by tightening environmental regulations on phenolic compounds, which are pushing manufacturers toward lower-residual formulations and driving qualification costs for end users.
Supply-side dynamics, including volatility in cresol feedstock prices from coal-tar distillation and synthetic cresol production, add cost uncertainty. The baseline scenario for the global cresol-derived frothers market anticipates a 4.2% CAGR from 2026 to 2035, with the market index rising to 150 (2025=100) by the end of the forecast period. This outlook assumes continued growth in global copper and zinc mine production, driven by electrification, renewable energy infrastructure, and electronics manufacturing. Cresol-derived frothers are expected to maintain their share of the synthetic frother market, supported by their stable foam performance and selectivity in complex ore bodies.
However, substitution pressure from ester-based and polyglycol alternatives is projected to erode the cresol-derived segment share by 2–4 percentage points by 2035, as environmental regulations favor more benign chemistries. The baseline scenario also incorporates a gradual shift toward high-purity, low-residual cresol formulations, particularly in Europe and North America, where discharge limits are tightening. Supply-chain diversification, including increased use of synthetic cresol feedstocks, is expected to stabilize price baselines and reduce regional production advantages.
