articles.title: November NG Slips to $2.975 as Mild Weather Masks 45 Bcf Storage Surplus and First-Ever 20 Bcf/d LNG Demand - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: November NG Slips to $2.975 as Mild Weather Masks 45 Bcf Storage Surplus and First-Ever 20 Bcf/d LNG Demand  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- U.S. LNG feedgas hit a record 20.7 Bcf/d on Monday, crossing 20 Bcf/d for the first time.
- The storage surplus to the five-year average fell from 68 Bcf to 45 Bcf in the week to October 9.
- November natural gas futures fell 8.3 cents to $2.975, breaking below $3.00 on mild weather.
November natural gas futures on NYMEX traded at $2.975 per MMBtu at 11:45 a.m. in New York on Tuesday, down 8.3 cents, or 2.7%, from Monday’s settlement near $3.058. The prompt contract tested below $3.00 support in early trade and stayed there through midday. Henry Hub spot gas averaged $3.121 in morning trading, a premium of 14.6 cents to the futures contract. The November contract had settled at $3.24 on October 15 and touched $3.30 earlier in the month as Hurricane Isaias approached the Gulf. From that peak, the contract has lost 32.5 cents, or 9.8%, in under two weeks.
The thesis for this forecast is direct. The break below $3.00 is a weather-driven dip inside a market that is tightening structurally, not the start of a new downtrend. Mild shoulder-season forecasts and recovering production are weighing on the prompt month right now. Against that, feedgas to U.S. LNG export terminals hit a record 20.7 Bcf/d on Monday, surpassing 20 Bcf/d for the first time. The storage surplus to the five-year average has narrowed from 68 Bcf to 45 Bcf in a week. South Central salt storage sits 15.4% below its five-year average. The fundamentals that matter for January are getting tighter while the weather that matters for late October is getting softer.
The longer view frames the move. Natural gas is up 6.1% over the past month but 13.4% lower than a year ago. The November contract made its first prompt-month settlement at $3.01 on September 29, rose to $3.24 by October 15, and has now returned below that starting level. Month to date through October 15, November futures averaged $3.15 per MMBtu. Tuesday’s $2.975 sits 5.6% below that average.
Trading volume has fallen since late September. Thin participation amplifies weather-driven moves, which explains part of the sharp two-day slide from $3.24 to below $3.00. Deferred contracts have held up better than the prompt month, which shows that traders are selling November’s mild weather while protecting their winter exposure.
The levels that matter are clear. Support sits at $2.95, then $2.90 and $2.85. Resistance sits at $3.058, Monday’s settlement, then $3.20, $3.24 and the $3.30 October high. The November contract expires on October 28, so the prompt-month dynamics will shift to December within six sessions.
Bearish Weather Pushed November Below Technical Support
The weather is the single biggest reason for Tuesday’s decline. Strong production and benign shoulder-season forecasts weighed on futures from the opening bell. The latest outlooks call for weaker-than-normal heating demand across the northern United States into late October, removing the early-season furnace demand that traders had begun to price.
The shift has been fast. The previous week brought northern chills that ignited furnaces and southern heat that kept air conditioners running, which pushed physical weekly prices higher. That combination of heating and cooling demand supported the November contract above $3.20. The new forecasts remove both. With neither heating nor cooling demand elevated, late October falls into the shoulder-season demand lull.
Power demand confirms the weakness. Gas burned for power generation fell 5.8 Bcf/d week over week. Mild temperatures reduce electricity demand, and blustery winds have lifted wind generation, which displaces gas-fired power. Strong wind output is one reason storage injections are expected to pick up in the coming week.
The decline started on Monday. Natural gas futures retreated even as LNG feedgas demand hit a record, with weaker heating demand expectations and the prospect of recovering production weighing on nearby contracts. November settled below technical support on Monday, which set up Tuesday’s follow-through break below $3.00. Futures fell from mid-October highs near $3.30 to about $3.06 by Monday’s close.
The demand outlook improves into November. Total U.S. demand, including exports, is expected to rise as colder weather arrives in early November, a normal seasonal pattern. Heating demand typically ramps sharply through November as the withdrawal season begins. The question for the November contract is whether that ramp starts before expiry on October 28. Current forecasts say it does not.
Weather-driven moves in late October tend to reverse once the first cold snap arrives. Every heating season begins with a shoulder period, and the timing of the first major cold outbreak varies by weeks from year to year. Traders who sold November on mild forecasts are betting that the cold arrives late. Traders holding December and January are betting it arrives on schedule.
LNG Feedgas Crossed 20 Bcf/d for the First Time
The most important structural development in U.S. natural gas came on Monday. Feedgas to U.S. LNG export terminals reached a record 20.7 Bcf/d, surpassing 20 Bcf/d for the first time. A decade after the first LNG cargo from the Lower 48 left Sabine Pass, export demand has become the largest single source of growth in U.S. gas consumption.
The infrastructure behind that number is expanding. The United States now has eight operating LNG terminals, with seven more under construction. Feedgas averaged about 18.2 Bcf/d in the week ending October 11, up 0.4 Bcf/d from the prior week, as Freeport and Cove Point returned from maintenance. Freeport LNG Train 2 was down for maintenance from October 2 to 8, and Cove Point was down for annual maintenance from September 19 until it returned to full operations on October 12.
Golden Pass is the key new contributor. The commissioning terminal took in less than 300 MMcf/d at the start of the week ending October 11 but reached record levels above 600 MMcf/d over the following weekend. October has seen intake days as high as 690 MMcf/d. Between April and the end of September, feedgas to Golden Pass’s commissioning train averaged just 300 MMcf/d, with periods when it took little or no gas. The ramp-up at Golden Pass is one of the main reasons feedgas crossed 20 Bcf/d.
Other projects are adding volume. Plaquemines LNG and Corpus Christi Stage 3 have ramped up, and LNG Canada has begun initial commissioning flows. U.S. LNG exports averaged 17.4 Bcf/d in the first half of 2026, up 23% from the first half of 2025. Export capacity reached 18.3 Bcf/d in April, up from 15.4 Bcf/d in October 2025. U.S. LNG exports are on track to exceed 120 million tonnes in 2026.
The year-to-date comparison shows the scale of the shift. Feedgas volumes have averaged 2.4 Bcf/d higher through October 14 than in the same period of 2025, a 15.7% increase. For October month to date, volumes are nearly 8% higher than a year ago.
The record is unlikely to hold for long. With Golden Pass ramping and winter demand for LNG rising in Europe and Asia, feedgas is heading into another record-breaking winter. Each additional Bcf/d of LNG demand removes gas that would otherwise go into storage, which tightens the domestic balance through the withdrawal season.
Storage Surplus Shrinks to 45 Bcf as South Central Salt Runs 15.4% Low
The storage data shows a market that is tighter than the price suggests. U.S. Lower 48 working gas rose 67 Bcf to 3,567 Bcf in the week ending October 9, according to the Energy Information Administration’s weekly report. The injection was 23 Bcf below the five-year average of 90 Bcf for the same week. The smaller build pushed futures up 37 ticks on the release.
The surplus to normal is shrinking. Inventories stood 45 Bcf, or 1.3%, above the five-year average of 3,522 Bcf. A week earlier, the surplus was 68 Bcf, or 2.0%. In one week, a fifth of the cushion disappeared. Stocks were 143 Bcf below the level a year earlier, widening from a 130 Bcf deficit the week before.
The prior week shows the trend. The EIA reported an 85 Bcf injection for the week ending October 2, the largest since late June, which lifted stocks to 3,500 Bcf. That build exceeded the 79 Bcf estimate but still fell short of the 96 Bcf five-year average. The week before brought a 64 Bcf build against an 80 Bcf average. Injections have run below normal for three straight weeks.
The South Central region is the pressure point. South Central salt storage, the most flexible and responsive storage in the country, held 236 Bcf in the week ending October 9. That level is 15.4% below the five-year average and 21.9% below a year earlier. Salt caverns can inject and withdraw gas quickly, which makes them critical for managing short-term demand spikes in winter. Nonsalt storage in the region held 861 Bcf, 0.9% below the five-year average.
The low salt levels sit right next to the LNG terminals. Most U.S. export terminals are on the Gulf Coast, where South Central storage is concentrated. Record feedgas is drawing gas from the same region where flexible storage is tightest.
The next report arrives Thursday. Estimates for the week ending October 16 point to an 82 Bcf injection, against 86 Bcf a year earlier and a five-year average of 87 Bcf. The range of estimates runs from 72 to 87 Bcf. An 82 Bcf build would narrow the surplus by another 5 Bcf. An injection near the low end at 72 Bcf would cut the surplus to around 30 Bcf and likely lift prices.
Production Fell From 113.3 Bcf/d Records to an Eight-Month Low
The supply side has been volatile, and its recovery is part of what pushed futures below $3.00. Lower 48 natural gas production hit record highs of 113.3 Bcf/d in August and September. In October, output averaged between 110.6 and 111.3 Bcf/d, depending on the measure. On October 13, daily output was on track to drop to an eight-month low of around 107.1 Bcf/d.

articles.title: Copper Supply Gap Could Reach 20 Million Metric Tons by 2050 - TOKENPOST
articles.summary: Copper Supply Gap Could Reach 20 Million Metric Tons by 2050  TOKENPOST
articles.full_text:
Global copper demand is projected to outpace supply starting in 2028, with the gap potentially reaching 20 million metric tons by 2050 as electrified transport and power grids need more metal.
The 2050 shortfall would represent 44% of projected worldwide demand. Bridging it would require an estimated $332 billion in new mine investment.
Copper demand is projected to grow 61% from 2026 to 2050, reaching nearly 46 million tons. Demand from electrified transport is expected to rise 244% to 11.4 million tons over the same period. Those figures measure expected demand, which may exceed the amount producers can supply.
Electrified transport alone would account for roughly one-quarter of projected copper demand in 2050. Power grids and other uses would draw on the same supply base, adding to the need for mining capacity as transport demand grows.
Copper stands apart from the other nine materials in the long-term assessment. Aluminum, cobalt, graphite, lithium, manganese, nickel, platinum, palladium and steel are expected to have enough supply capacity through 2050 if producers continue developing mines and replacing depleted reserves. Copper is the only material in the group with a projected shortage.
The demand figures also show why transport is a major part of the challenge. Its projected 244% increase is much steeper than the 61% rise in overall copper demand. Producers would need to serve that growth while supplying the metal used in grids and other applications.
Earlier coverage of four copper miners exposed to tightening supply examined individual producers. The new projection puts a global figure on the longer-term gap between copper demand and available supply.
Mine development limits how quickly producers can respond. New mines take 17 years on average to begin operating, while declining ore quality and years of insufficient exploration spending make it harder to expand output. The projected deficit would begin well before a mine started today would typically enter production.

articles.title: Copper Outperforms Gold as AI Infrastructure, Defense Spending Drive Global Race for Supplies - Tekedia
articles.summary: Copper Outperforms Gold as AI Infrastructure, Defense Spending Drive Global Race for Supplies  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
Copper is gaining strategic importance as governments and industries compete to secure supplies of the industrial metal, with investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, electricity grids and national defense creating new sources of demand.
The shift is strengthening the outlook for copper miners even as concerns over the sustainability of AI spending weigh on technology stocks.
Copper has risen 15.8% year to date and more than 30% over the past 12 months, outperforming gold as investors focus on the metal’s role in supporting technological development, industrial expansion and national security. By comparison, gold futures have fallen 4.11% this year and 4.52% over the past 12 months, while spot gold has declined 4% year to date and 4.89% over the past year.

The divergence is considered an indication of a shift in investor priorities. While gold traditionally attracts demand as a store of value during periods of economic and geopolitical uncertainty, copper is benefiting from expectations that the expansion of digital infrastructure, electrification and defense capabilities will require sustained investment in physical assets.
Speaking to CNBC’s Squawk Box Europe as LME Week, the global metals industry’s annual gathering, began in London on Monday, Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin said governments and businesses were increasingly treating access to metals as a strategic priority.
Countries, regions and industries are seeking reliable supplies to support national security, economic growth and technology infrastructure, Melvin said, helping underpin copper prices.
“It’s certainly a good time to be in copper mining globally, and specifically in the United States,” said Melvin, whose Arizona-based mining and exploration company focuses on copper, gold, silver, nickel and cobalt.
“We’re really in a world right now where the metals that we used to refer to, and still do, as critical metals are really becoming strategic metals, in every sense of the word,” he added.
Copper is no longer valued solely for its role in conventional industrial production. Its importance to power transmission, electronics, transportation, and the construction of data centers is making dependable access to the metal a growing economic and geopolitical concern.
Copper’s outlook is strengthening as the build-out of AI infrastructure adds to demand from established industrial sectors. Data centers require extensive electrical systems, while the power generation and transmission infrastructure needed to support them adds another layer of copper consumption.
The demand is emerging at a time when investors are questioning whether the enormous capital commitments made by major technology companies will generate sufficient returns. Recent volatility in technology stocks has exposed concerns about AI valuations, the scale of hyperscaler investment and the possibility that spending could eventually slow.
Melvin, however, argued that fluctuations in financial-market sentiment should not be confused with a deterioration in the underlying demand for copper.
“It’s a new pocket of demand, and it really is almost an inelastic demand for copper,” he said, referring to the technology sector’s requirements for the metal.
“It’s hard to think that one of these large-scale technology companies is going to make an investment decision on a hyperscale data center based on the cost of copper.”
His argument is that copper represents a necessary input into infrastructure projects whose overall costs and strategic importance extend far beyond the price of any single material. If companies remain committed to expanding computing capacity, relatively higher copper prices may not be sufficient to derail projects that depend on extensive electrical infrastructure.
That does not make demand entirely immune to a slowdown. If technology companies reduce capital expenditure, delay projects or reassess expected returns, the pace of new construction could weaken. But Melvin’s assessment suggests that short-term changes in equity valuations do not necessarily invalidate longer-term investment plans.
He also identified national security and defense spending as another source of demand that could support the market, broadening copper’s exposure beyond commercial technology investment.
“That same inelasticity applies to another demand pocket that’s emerging, which is national security, national defense budgets,” Melvin said.
“There certainly has been a bit of a retrench, a retreat, in those [tech] valuations. But two things can be true at the same time — you can have a capital market move in sentiment on equity values… but it can also be true that those industries are growing, and they’re going to be a source of incremental demand for our metal.”
The combination of AI infrastructure and defense expenditure could therefore make copper demand less dependent on traditional construction and manufacturing cycles.
US Tariff Uncertainty Tightens The Supply Picture
Trade policy is adding another source of uncertainty to the copper market. The United States has been considering tariffs on refined copper, raising questions about where inventories will be held and whether metal accumulated in the country will remain accessible to buyers elsewhere.
In 2025, the US Commerce Department recommended a 15% tariff beginning January 1, 2027. A final decision on the proposed levy has not been publicly announced, leaving traders and investors to account for the possibility of changes in trade flows.
The prospect of tariffs has encouraged a large share of global copper stocks to be stored in the United States, according to Iain Pyle, senior investment director at Aberdeen Investments and co-manager of the abrdn Future Minerals Fund.
“Because of the potential for US tariffs, a large share of the world’s copper is now stored in the US, and it isn’t clear those stocks will be available to the rest of the market,” Pyle said.
The concentration of inventories in the United States could tighten supplies available to buyers in other regions, particularly if tariff implementation makes it more expensive to move copper across borders. The resulting uncertainty can influence prices even before a policy decision is finalized, as market participants adjust purchasing and inventory strategies in anticipation of potential trade barriers.
Conditions in China, a major consumer of industrial metals, are adding to concerns about availability.
“At the same time, Chinese inventories look exceptionally low and premiums there are rising,” Pyle said.
Low inventories and rising premiums can indicate that buyers are competing more aggressively for immediately available material. If demand remains firm while accessible stocks decline, prices may need to rise further to encourage additional production, investment and recycling.
In an October 15 note, Pyle described copper as the “clearest example” of a market where supply cannot keep pace with demand. He argued that “higher incentives will be needed in the form of sustained higher copper prices.”
Such incentives are important because expanding mine supply typically requires substantial capital, lengthy development periods, and regulatory approvals. Higher prices can improve the economics of new projects, but they do not guarantee that additional production will become available quickly enough to ease near-term shortages.
Pyle nevertheless warned that tariff announcements could trigger a temporary reversal in prices, depending on the final policy and its implications for inventory movements.
“There is still some risk of a pullback around tariff announcements, but we see the underlying fundamentals as clearly bullish, and the potential for a spike in prices has increased,” he said.
Copper’s rally now rests on two related forces: expectations of sustained demand growth and uncertainty over the availability of supply. AI infrastructure and defense spending are expanding the metal’s strategic role, while trade policy and low inventories are complicating the distribution of existing stocks.

articles.full_text:
Ethiopia has taken another step toward expanding its natural gas processing capacity after China’s GCL Group and Jurong Group signed a contract to advance the second phase of the Ogaden liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in the country’s Somali Region.
The agreement was signed on October 16, 2026, at Ethiopia’s Ministry of Mines, bringing together GCL Energy Investment Co., Ltd., a subsidiary of GCL Group, and Jurong Group (Holdings) Co., Ltd. The contract covers construction and entrusted processing services for the LNG development based on the Calub gas field in the Ogaden Basin.
The signing was witnessed by Ethiopian government officials. Fu Zhidong, president of GCL’s liquefaction and refining business division in Ethiopia, and Yi Min, vice president of Jurong Group, signed on behalf of the respective companies. The Ministry of Mines has called for construction of the first module under Phase II to begin as soon as possible.
The agreement follows a strategic cooperation framework signed by the two companies in May 2026. It is intended to advance construction of the gas liquefaction facilities. This is while strengthening supporting infrastructure, storage, transportation and potential international trading channels.
Second phase of Ogaden LNG project to expand Ethiopia’s LNG production
The latest agreement builds on the first phase of the Ogaden LNG project. GCL commissioned Calub’s first phase in Ethiopia’s Somali Region on October 2, 2025. The initial modular plant was designed to process approximately 200,000 cubic meters of natural gas daily. It was also set to produce about 50,000 tons of LNG annually.
The facility marked a milestone in Ethiopia’s efforts to develop its domestic natural gas resources and supply industrial customers with locally produced fuel. The first phase primarily targets industrial parks and other domestic end users. On the other hand, the second phase is intended to support expanded production and access to international export markets.
The Phase II development was launched alongside other oil and gas initiatives in October 2025. This includes natural gas-fired power generation and oil refining projects. However, the latest agreement does not disclose the contract value. It also does not disclose the additional LNG production capacity covered by the contract, or a completion date.
Infrastructure development central to the project
Beyond the liquefaction plant itself, the second phase is expected to require supporting infrastructure. This will be used for handling, storing and transporting natural gas and LNG. Additionally, Jurong Group has indicated that it will contribute expertise in liquefaction infrastructure and project management. The company will also contribute to storage, transportation and international trade, working alongside GCL to develop the wider project infrastructure.
These components will be important. They will determine how effectively Ethiopia can move beyond producing natural gas to supplying larger domestic markets and potentially reaching overseas buyers.
The development also fits into GCL’s broader plans for Ethiopia’s oil and gas sector. This includes natural gas processing, power generation and downstream industrial applications. The company has also positioned the Ogaden Basin LNG project as a foundation for developing an integrated domestic gas value chain. This is alongside the US$660 million refined petroleum products Ethiopia-Djibouti pipeline project launched in September 2026.
Ogaden gas development linked to Ethiopia’s industrial ambitions
Ethiopia is seeking to use its natural gas resources to support industrialization and improve domestic energy supply. The country also seeks to reduce reliance on imported energy products. The Ogaden Basin’s Calub and Hilala gas fields are central to these ambitions.
One related initiative is the planned fertilizer complex in Gode, Somali Region. In March 2026, GCL and Dangote Group announced a 25-year natural gas supply agreement valued at approximately US$4.2 billion to support the proposed fertilizer facility. The arrangement also includes plans for a dedicated 108-kilometre gas pipeline linking the Calub gas field to the fertilizer production base in Gode.
The proposed fertilizer plant is also designed to produce approximately three million tons annually. It is expected to begin operations in 2029. If delivered as planned, the project could establish a major domestic market for Ethiopian natural gas. This is while supporting fertilizer production and agricultural supply chains.
The LNG expansion and fertilizer development therefore represent complementary parts of Ethiopia’s wider strategy to turn its gas resources into industrial output, energy supplies and export revenue.
Outlook for the Ogaden LNG project
The signing of the Phase II contract marks a further step in moving Ethiopia’s Ogaden gas development. It sets pace for the project to advance from initial production toward larger-scale processing and commercialization. The immediate priority is to advance construction of the first module and establish the infrastructure required to support the expanded project.
However, the development’s eventual contribution will depend on construction progress and financing. Gas supply, transport infrastructure and the establishment of reliable markets also factor in. International LNG sales will also require commercially viable logistics and export arrangements, details of which have yet to be fully disclosed.
If the expansion proceeds successfully, the Ogaden project could become an important component of Ethiopia’s emerging natural gas industry. It would connect domestic gas resources with power generation, manufacturing, fertilizer production and potential international markets.

articles.title: Global copper market will require $332 billion in investment by 2050 - Open4business.com.ua.
articles.summary: Global copper market will require $332 billion in investment by 2050  Open4business.com.ua.
articles.full_text:
The global copper industry will need approximately $332 billion in new investment in mining projects by 2050 to prevent a large-scale shortage of the metal, which could reach 20 million tonnes per year, or 44% of projected demand. This is stated in the Transition Metals Outlook 2026 study by analytical company BloombergNEF (BNEF), published on October 20, 2026.
According to the forecast, the global copper market could face a deficit as early as 2028, as the expansion of mining capacity lags behind consumption growth. The main drivers of increasing demand will be the electrification of transport, modernization of power grids, industrial development, and infrastructure construction.
BNEF analysts expect global copper consumption to increase by 61% by 2050 compared with 2026, reaching almost 46 million tonnes.
At the same time, demand for copper associated with the electrification of the economy will grow by 89%, to 23.3 million tonnes. Thus, these areas will account for more than half of global metal consumption.
Electric transportation will become the fastest-growing segment. Copper use in electric cars, electric trucks, buses, and related infrastructure will increase by 244%, reaching 11.4 million tonnes by the middle of the century.
Copper is essential for the production of electric motors, inverters, batteries, high-voltage wiring, and charging stations. In addition, the metal is widely used in construction, industrial equipment, electrical grids, and consumer electronics.
According to BloombergNEF estimates, existing global copper ore reserves are sufficient to meet long-term needs, but the problem lies in the insufficient pace of developing new deposits and expanding existing operations.
The average period from the start of project development to the commissioning of a new copper mine is approximately 17 years. As a result, even with the necessary $332 billion in investment, the metal shortage could persist until at least 2043.
Additional challenges arise from declining copper grades in mined ore, rising production costs, and insufficient funding for geological exploration in previous years.
Without new capital investment, global copper supply could decline by 14.5%, from 30 million tonnes in 2026 to 25.7 million tonnes in 2050. The development of copper scrap recycling will partially offset the decline in primary production but will not be able to completely eliminate the projected shortage.
Chile, according to BloombergNEF’s forecast, will retain its status as the largest producer of primary copper. However, production in the country could decline from 5.8 million tonnes in 2026 to 4.8 million tonnes in 2050.
Despite the decline in absolute production volumes, Chile’s share of global primary copper production could increase from 24% to 28%, as reductions in other countries will be more significant.
Analysts warn that a prolonged copper shortage could lead to higher global prices and increased costs for energy equipment, electric transportation, and infrastructure projects. In certain segments, manufacturers may be forced to make greater use of alternative materials.
Martin Tengler, head of metals and mining research at BloombergNEF, noted that the situation regarding the supply of raw materials to the global economy has changed significantly compared with previous forecasts.
According to him, the development of new production capacity and improvements in battery technologies have reduced the risks of shortages of most energy transition metals. However, the main challenge is becoming ensuring the availability of the necessary materials in specific regions and at the required times.
At the same time, copper remains the main exception to the overall trend of improving forecasts.
According to Transition Metals Outlook 2026, nine of the ten metals and materials studied could potentially have sufficient production capacity by 2050, provided investment continues and depleted reserves are replaced.
In particular, global lithium consumption is expected to nearly triple, from 1.6 million to 4.8 million tonnes of lithium carbonate equivalent, while demand for graphite will more than double, from 3.3 million to 6.9 million tonnes.
At the same time, the increasing adoption of lithium iron phosphate batteries is reducing the expected need for nickel and cobalt compared with previous forecasts.
China continues to dominate the processing of energy transition metals. According to BloombergNEF, for eight of the ten materials studied, more than half of global processing capacity is concentrated in a single country, and for seven of these materials, that country is China.

articles.title: Wars are Driving New LNG Projects Across Texas & Louisiana Gulf Coast - deceleration.news
articles.summary: Wars are Driving New LNG Projects Across Texas & Louisiana Gulf Coast  deceleration.news
articles.full_text:
Over the last 14 months, liquefied natural gas (LNG) companies have proposed new expansion projects at seven gas export terminals along the Gulf Coast, encouraged in part by wars in the Middle East and Ukraine that have boosted the market for U.S. LNG shipments.
Three of the expanding terminals are in Louisiana, including southeast of New Orleans at the Plaquemines LNG terminal; and in Cameron, in southwest Louisiana, at the CP2 and Commonwealth LNG terminals, according to public records available in the Oil & Gas Watch database. Four expanding terminals are located in Texas, near Port Arthur, Brownsville, and Corpus Christi.
If built, these new expansions would increase by about 14 percent, or 75 million metric tons per year, the capacity of U.S. LNG export terminals that are operating, under construction, or previously proposed. The expansions and associated pipelines could also damage hundreds of acres of fragile coastal wetlands and release millions of tons of greenhouse gases, according to permit applications.
“These gas export facilities are a radical transformation of the Louisiana coast,” said Anne Rolfes, director of the Louisiana Bucket Brigade. 
“This coastal area, including our wetlands, protects south Louisiana from storms, a crucial buffer as hurricanes get more fierce. Now that protection is paved over, transformed into concrete so that an out-of-state corporation can make money.” 
Developers of the LNG projects argue that the wars in Iran and Ukraine are contributing to increasing market demand overseas for U.S. LNG exports, and the new expansions of Gulf Coast export terminals would help meet that rising need.
“Recent disruptions to LNG exports through the Strait of Hormuz are increasing demand for LNG cargoes from outside the strait,” Venture Global, which is building the CP2 LNG expansion project near Cameron, Louisiana, said in its May 26, 2026, application to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
Overall, nine LNG export terminals have been built across the U.S. over the last ten years. The industry’s rise was driven by the proliferation of new drilling techniques, including hydraulic fracturing and horizontal drilling, which dramatically expanded production of natural gas from shale rock formations.
The new expansions at seven LNG terminals, proposed since August 2025, would not be completed for several years.  The largest expansions are proposed at the Port Arthur LNG Terminal in Port Arthur, Texas; the CP2 LNG Terminal in Cameron, Louisiana; and the Plaquemines LNG Terminal in Port Sulphur, Louisiana. 
This new wave of expansions are on top of projects to build 24 new or expanded LNG terminals that were previously proposed, before August 2025, along the Gulf Coast, Alaska, and in other states, according to public records in the Oil & Gas Watch database.
The boom started in Louisiana, which has been an epicenter of the LNG industry. The first export of LNG from the U.S. came in 2016 from Cheniere Energy’s Sabine Pass Liquefaction Terminal located in Cameron Parish, in far southwestern Louisiana.
Since then, U.S. LNG exports have grown into a $44 billion annual industry that, within the next five years, has the potential to become the second largest net export from the U.S., behind only civilian aircrafts and parts, according to an estimate by S&P Global Energy.
As wars overseas continue to destabilize global energy markets, Wall Street investors are reportedly eager to fund U.S. LNG export opportunities that are perceived as more reliable and stable than LNG coming out of Russia or the Middle East.
One of the expansions is of the Venture Global CP2 LNG Terminal under construction about an hour south of Lake Charles in Cameron, on the Gulf Coast. The terminal, as originally proposed, would have had a processing capacity of 28 million metric tons of liquified natural gas per year.
But then in June 2026, Venture Global received permission to increase this terminal’s capacity by seven million metric tons per year. On top of that, Venture Global also submitted an application in May of 2026 seeking approval to increase the terminal’s export capacity by an additional 11.7 million metric tons per year.
The company’s Chief Executive Officer, Mike Sabel, said that Venture Global is positioning itself to become the largest exporter of LNG in the U.S.
“We will build on the strong construction progress already underway and deliver reliable American LNG to customers around the world,” Sabel said in a press release. 
But Breon Robinson, the Southwest Louisiana Organizer of Healthy Gulf, a nonprofit organization, said that the scale and the pace of the construction projects are threatening radical changes along the Gulf Coast.
“What’s especially concerning is the trajectory we’re seeing,” Robinson said. Regulators should “stop looking at these projects as isolated developments and start asking what the cumulative impact of continually expanding LNG infrastructure means for our communities, our environment, and Louisiana’s long-term future.”
The potential emissions of the expansions are significant. The CP2 expansion project alone could release more than 4.8 million tons of greenhouse gases per year, according to permit applications and public records. That would be the equivalent of the carbon dioxide from roughly one million cars and trucks driven for a year.
“Southwest Louisiana is already living with the health impacts, the traffic, and the loss of fishing grounds from the terminals we have, and families are being asked to absorb even more,” said James Hiatt, Executive Director of For a Better Bayou. 
“Regulators keep approving these expansions one piece at a time while the people of the Gulf Coast live with the whole thing.  
Venture Global has also proposed a similar expansion at another LNG terminal: the Plaquemines LNG Terminal, on the west bank of the Mississippi River about 25 miles southeast of New Orleans.
As planned originally, the facility would have been capable of producing 24 million tons of liquefied natural gas per year. But Venture Global has since applied for various expansions that would almost triple this capacity to 66 million metric tons of LNG per year.
These expansions are not limited to Louisiana. Similar proposals are also being announced for LNG terminals in Texas. One example is the Port Arthur LNG Export Terminal in East Texas, which is already under construction and could process up to 27 million metric tons of LNG per year. But in September of 2026, Sempra announced plans to build an expansion of the terminal that would double the facility’s processing capacity, bringing it to a total of 54 million metric tons of LNG per year, according to permit documents.
Impacts from these projects extend beyond the projects themselves to associated infrastructure, including pipelines.
The Cloud Connector, a proposed 165-mile pipeline that would transport natural gas to the Plaquemines LNG Terminal, is expected to damage up to 1,428 acres of wetlands, according to public records. Despite these impacts, the public was only given 11 days to notice to submit public comments – instead of the normal 30-day public comment period – because of expedited “energy emergency” procedures enacted by the Trump Administration.
Wetlands are a shrinking resource in Louisiana. The Bayou State has lost close to 2,000 square miles of land since the 1930s, according to the Louisiana Coastal Protection and Restoration Authority.

articles.title: Economics of Green Hydrogen: When and how will it be competitive?: Sudeep Maheshwari & Sanchit Makhija, Partner, Kearney - Indian Chemical News
articles.summary: Economics of Green Hydrogen: When and how will it be competitive?: Sudeep Maheshwari & Sanchit Makhija, Partner, Kearney  Indian Chemical News
articles.full_text:
Green hydrogen is still an evolving sector and will require strong, coordinated support across the ecosystem to become competitive at scale in India
Green hydrogen is moved slowly from concept to centrepiece in global decarbonization strategies. Governments see it as essential for net-zero ambitions while industrial players view it as a pathway to decarbonize processes that electricity alone cannot reach. Yet, a central question remains unresolved: when, where, and how will green hydrogen become economically competitive?
The answer is nuanced. Green hydrogen will not become competitive everywhere at once, nor across all applications simultaneously. Instead, competitiveness will emerge first in specific geographies, sectors, and use cases—driven by a combination of renewable power economics, technology learning, policy design, and financing structures. This pattern is particularly evident in India, where structural advantages coexist with practical constraints. India is expected to play a structural role in green hydrogen global ecosystem. It has advantages of largest integrated grid in the world, backed by low cost of renewable energy potential and strong policy intent from the government to enhance energy security for the country. In addition, high cost of gas also makes gap lower vs. green hydrogen. However, multiple challenges exist which need to be addressed to define the economics for Green hydrogen in India going forward.
Green Hydrogen: Cost gap that needs to be addressed for India
Cost of Green H2 is fundamentally determined by three key factors- price of clean electricity, electrolyser capital costs & its utilization rates and financing for the project. Together these determine the extent of cost gaps we see in India/ globally from conventional H2/ alternate fuels.
Electricity dominates the cost structure: Green H2 production is a power intensive process with requirement of 50-55 kWh of electricity per kilogram of hydrogen depending upon technology and efficiency. In India, renewables have been fairly competitive globally (ranging from Rs. 2.5-3.8/kWh depending upon the technology/ location). However, over the last 3 years, renewable tariffs have been rising consistently due to ALMM restrictions on the regulatory side, increase in equipment costs, cautious approach on CUFs by developers and lenders leading to higher cost of capital. In addition, co-location of renewables, access to banking and financing mechanisms, clear rules on grid supplied power in lines with global requirements critical to influence operating hours.
Capital intensity of electrolysers and utilization are critical: Electrolysers are capital intensive assets. In India, electrolyser domestic manufacturing is rising, however currently its exposed to global supply chains and currency risks. In future, backed by scaling, standardization, stack life improvements, electrolysers can have significantly lower costs. However, learning rates materialize only when deployment is sustained and supply chain mature. Stop start signals on policy can delay the cost reductions & keep “first of its kind” premiums high. In addition, in case electrolyzers run on low capacity factors on account of renewable power being intermittent or grid access being constrained, costs for the hydrogen rises further.
Financing costs and structures need addressal: Green Hydrogen is an emerging sector where risks on projects are not completely understood due to limited on-ground projects. By nature, these projects also involve large upfront investment, long payment periods and limited long term off taker agreements. Indian capital markets have been hesitant to fund such projects- thereby increasing costs and limited flexibility on structures for meeting project needs.
In addition to these challenges, it’s also critical to address the overall supply chain costs- including compressors, storage, transport and conversion into derivatives such as ammonia/ methanol. In India, where hydrogen infrastructure is limited, these downstream costs can rival productions costs especially for distributed/ export oriented projects
Path for Competitiveness in India
In our view, India can follow a 4 pronged approach for addressing the competitiveness of green hydrogen. This over the coming 3-5 years can enhance India’s chances to reach 5 MMTPA targets for domestic production and 10 per cent of global green hydrogen demand. It’s imperative that India progresses all these imperatives in parallel to meet the pace of global developments and needs for meeting its Net Zero targets.
Building hub & valley infrastructure to drive scale and reducing the costs of hydrogen production as supply chain mature. This would involve multiple activities including expediting plans on developing three to four 1-MMPTA+ eastern & western coast hubs, fast tracking 3-5 high priority ports anchored for GH2 exports with adequate ammonia/ methanol storage, standardization of certifications (RFNBO/ non RFNBO) early and aligning with global (European/ US/ Japanese) benchmarks. In addition, allocation of high CUF sites for wind and solar projects is critical for enabling the environment for hub development. Overall, country needs to plan hydrogen corridors/ valleys for enabling scale in this area.
Domestic demand certainty via mandates/ standards/ public procurement: Accelerate ammonia and GH2 demand aggregation opportunities across Indian refinery and fertilizer space. In addition, push on methanol based opportunities such as diesel blending in the Indian domestic market through similar routes. In addition, imported urea can be replaced by green urea via domestic GH2 route. These would demonstrate viabilities as well as get large private investors/ developers in the space which would create a virtuous cycle of interest in the space.
GoI support for making GH2 competitive: This is a critical enabler for building the viability of Indian export oriented projects, especially in early days. Active engagement at G2G level for inclusion of Indian grid as a bidding zone in European standards, inclusion of carbon trading under bilateral Japanese / Korean agreements is key. State/ central level support as capex subsidies, waivers on electricity duty in the target states, push on inter/ intra state waivers on power transmission (charges & losses), push on production subsidies on domestic electrolyzer manufacturing can also enhance the viability of the GH2 product from India. In addition, existing provisions for SEZs for GH2 hubs and associated RE infrastructure can also help.
Green financing push customized for GH2 projects: Typically, GH2 and its derivative projects would have 10-12 year offtake agreements. This would require innovative structures on green financing to fund the projects. Indian NBFCs can take a lead in mobilizing global capital for these area and build the ecosystem for accessing th real risks for such GH2 projects. In addition, evaluating mezzanine funds/ short erm arrangement for construction phase at competitive rates would also enable faster movement. GH2 derivative linked bonds can also lead to active investor interest in this area.
In summary, green hydrogen is still an evolving sector and will require strong, coordinated support across the ecosystem to become competitive at scale in India. This includes sustained engagement from central and state governments, public and private developers, EPC contractors, electrolyser manufacturers, certification agencies, banks, and patient, long-term capital providers.
Financial institutions will need to adapt appraisal frameworks to reflect the unique risk profiles of GH₂ and derivative projects, while policy clarity and standardization will be essential to build investor confidence.
The next three to five years are critical for establishing hub infrastructure, supply chains, and market demand at scale. Timely and well-aligned interventions can create a virtuous cycle of scale, cost reduction, and investment. If executed effectively, India can emerge as a global leader in the green hydrogen ecosystem, while strengthening energy security and long-term industrial competitiveness.

While nine out of ten key energy transition metals are back on track to deliver sufficient supply by 2050, a total of $332 billion of investment is needed in new copper mines to avoid a looming copper deficit that could slow electrification, BloombergNEF said in its Transition Metals Outlook 2026 on Tuesday.
In recent years, supply of key energy transition metals has improved considerably, with the exception of copper, which is still expected to see a shortfall through 2050, unless billions of dollars are invested in new supply.
Lithium, graphite, cobalt, aluminum, nickel, manganese, steel, platinum, and palladium are all expected to have sufficient long-term supply capacity to support electrification through 2050, as global shortages have eased significantly, BNEF says.
However, copper remains the major exception in this group of critical metals.
BNEF expects a supply deficit in the global copper markets to begin in 2028 and widen to as much as 20 million metric tons by 2050. This deficit would be equivalent to 44% of projected global demand.
Meanwhile, global copper demand is expected to jump by 61% between 2026 and 2050, reaching nearly 46 million tons. Copper demand for electrified transport alone is forecast to soar by 244% to 11.4 million tons.
"The shortfall could push up prices, force manufacturers to use alternative materials and slow the deployment of electric vehicles, batteries and electricity grids," the research provider said.
"Even with the necessary investment, bringing new mines into operation takes an average of 17 years, meaning the shortfall could persist for decades," according to BNEF.
The outlook also found that despite the West's diversification efforts, China continues to dominate metals refining globally, which raises supply security concerns. Eight of the 10 materials studied have more than half their refining capacity concentrated in a single country; seven of these are in China, BNEF noted.

articles.title: Downside Pressure Deepens on PMET Resources Inc. Amid Broad Lithium Correction Risks and Cautious Near-Term Sentiment - kalkine.ca
articles.summary: Downside Pressure Deepens on PMET Resources Inc. Amid Broad Lithium Correction Risks and Cautious Near-Term Sentiment  kalkine.ca
articles.full_text:
Key Highlights:
- Persistent Downside Pressure: PMET shares experienced a notable session decline, closing down by 3.04% on October 19, 2026, driven by broad-based selling pressure and a cautious investor backdrop.
- Valuation Concerns: Elevated valuation dynamics relative to near-term cash generation leave the equity vulnerable to negative re-rating risks.
- Sector Headwinds: Sluggish pricing environments across critical battery minerals and broader commodity volatility continue to depress sentiment toward early-stage development assets.
- Financing and Capital Intensity: Substantial ongoing capital requirements for advanced-stage exploration and project advancement heighten market sensitivity to dilution and funding conditions.
Introduction
PMET Resources Inc.
(TSX:PMET) operates as a critical mineral exploration and development enterprise focused primarily on advancing its district-scale, wholly-owned Shaakichiuwaanaan property (formerly known as Corvette) located in the Eeyou Istchee James Bay region of Québec, Canada.
The company’s core business model centers on delineating and developing large-scale pegmatite-hosted lithium resources to supply the rapidly evolving North American electric vehicle and energy storage supply chain.
Principal operational activities are concentrated in northwestern Québec, an established yet logistically challenging mining jurisdiction.
Recently, the company’s shares have faced intensifying downward pressure, closing the session in the red with a 3.
04% pullback on October 19, 2026.
This retreat reflects a confluence of company-specific execution hurdles, waning risk appetite across the junior mining complex, and macro-level uncertainties.
Broader sector conditions remain burdened by persistent softness in lithium spot markets, which has sapped speculative momentum and driven institutional capital outflows from pre-revenue developers.
Furthermore, macroeconomic headwinds, including tighter financing conditions and volatile capital markets, continue to weigh heavily on early-stage resource equities.
As market participants demand tangible cash-flow visibility and lower execution risk, the current operating environment is likely to remain challenging for equities heavily reliant on future capital deployment.

Key Reasons Behind Decline
The recent correction in PMET Resources Inc. shares is rooted in a combination of negative investor sentiment, sector-wide weakness, and growing macroeconomic caution. Investor sentiment toward the lithium exploration sector has turned markedly defensive as market participants re-evaluate the near-term demand trajectory for electric vehicle battery raw materials. This shift has triggered noticeable institutional outflows and speculative selling across pre-production mining names, putting direct downward pressure on share prices. Compounding these sentiment-driven dynamics are growing concerns regarding declining earnings visibility and the capital-intensive nature of advancing large-scale mineral assets from study phases toward eventual construction. With broader commodity markets experiencing heightened volatility, investors have displayed a distinct aversion to assets requiring substantial near-term capital outlays without immediate commercial production horizons. Additionally, broader economic uncertainties, including shifting interest-rate expectations and persistent global growth concerns, have restricted risk capital availability for the junior mining sector, amplifying downward momentum during negative trading sessions.
Risks to Consider
Investors evaluating PMET Resources Inc. must navigate a complex array of structural and operational risks that could influence future share-price performance. Primary among these is funding risk; the substantial capital required to complete ongoing exploration, environmental assessments, and engineering studies exposes the company to potential equity dilution or unfavorable financing terms if market conditions remain subdued. Operational execution issues, including potential project delays, permitting hurdles, or unexpected cost inflation related to remote northern infrastructure development, represent additional threats to shareholder value. Furthermore, ongoing commodity price volatility in the global lithium market directly impacts the perceived economic viability of large-scale development projects, potentially altering long-term cash generation projections. Macroeconomic factors such as persistent interest-rate sensitivity and broader industrial demand slowdowns could further impair liquidity and dampen investor appetite, limiting the company's strategic flexibility in navigating capital markets.
Valuation Perspective
Assessing the valuation of PMET Resources Inc. requires a careful distinction between the company's undeniable long-term fundamental resource potential and its near-term valuation vulnerabilities. While the district-scale nature of the Shaakichiuwaanaan project offers significant strategic allure within the domestic battery supply chain, current market pricing appears demanding when weighed against the absence of near-term operating cash flows. Investor skepticism has grown around capital intensity and the extended timeline required to bring greenfield mineral projects into commercial production. Consequently, downside re-rating risk remains present, as current market expectations leave little margin for operational missteps or extended project timelines. The prevailing valuation profile suggests that future share-price appreciation will require flawless execution, sustained proof of resource expansion, and a broader rehabilitation of investor confidence in the battery metals sector.
Outlook
The forward-looking assessment for PMET Resources Inc. remains cautious and balanced, reflecting a tug-of-war between long-term strategic positioning and near-term macroeconomic headwinds. While the structural shift toward domestic critical mineral supply chains provides a supportive long-term backdrop, near-term operational risks, sector headwinds, and funding requirements dictate a prudent stance. For investor sentiment to sustainably improve, market participants will likely need to see concrete catalysts, including successful navigation of environmental permitting milestones, clearer visibility on capital funding structures, sustained optimization of engineering studies, and a broader stabilization in lithium commodity pricing trends. Until these fundamental milestones are decisively achieved, the equity is likely to remain sensitive to broader market volatility and shifting risk sentiment.

China is eager to avoid overcapacity in yet another clean energy sector as it looks to curb excess hydrogen production amid overheated investments in projects.
Over the past years, China, the world's top solar equipment manufacturer, has grappled with overcapacity and price wars in the solar sector amid booming installations and solar equipment exports. Battery manufacturing has also come under increased government scrutiny amid signs of overcapacity.
Now the country leading the global clean energy rollout is looking to avoid a repeat of the same mistakes in the hydrogen sector, too.
"Due to the overheated investment in certain aspects of the hydrogen sector, we are formulating a plan for the rational allocation of major projects," a senior official at the top economic planner, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), said at a Tuesday briefing, as carried by Bloomberg.
"Both the national and local governments should conduct in-depth analysis when organizing projects to avoid blind investment and waste of funds," NDRC's Ren Zhongbao added.
China boasts rapid deployment, ability to scale, and cost leadership in the clean hydrogen sector, according to a report by DNV from earlier this year.
At present, China accounts for around 60% of global electrolyzer deployment and investment decisions. Costs continue to decline due to sustained technology investment, local supply chains, and access to low-cost capital, DNV reckons.
"Production costs are roughly half those seen in many other markets, with projects scaling from tens to hundreds of megawatts within a few years," according to the analysts.
Competition among hydrogen manufacturers in China is fierce, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said last week.
In 2025, China's electrolyzer manufacturing capacity was 35 GW per year while demand was less than 2 GW.
"This substantial overcapacity has contributed to bidding below full cost, with awarded bids in auctions falling as low as USD 170/kW," IEA's analysts noted.
With clean hydrogen investments and projects in China booming, Beijing wants to avoid the mistakes in the solar and battery industries.

By: Nghiinomewa-vali Hangala
The developer of the Haib Copper Mine in southern Namibia has reported that the Definitive Feasibility Study (DFS) to guide the development of the copper mine will be completed by next year.
Koryx Copper, which is doing the metallurgical assessment of the reserve, announced this as part of their interim update on the Pre-Feasibility Study Progress for the project.
In mining, a DFS determines if the found mineral reserve is investment-grade, providing a detailed technical and financial basis for a decision to develop the mine and finance the project.
According to Koryx, their metallurgical program for the DFS is well underway, with drill core and pilot bulk metallurgical sample selection having commenced in August.
The sample selection is focused on building a comprehensive geo-metallurgical model for both comminution and flotation aspects of the Project during the DFS planned for 2027, the miners said.
The miners updated that their pre-feasibility study has met test work results near completion and is showing consistency with historical results, thus supporting PFS metallurgical assumptions and by-product recovery potential.
In terms of bulk water supply, once the DFS is reached, the developer/Koryx will sign a MoU with NamWater. An Infrastructure Development Agreement for the bulk water supply system will be developed.
The Orange River supply scheme was selected as the preferred, lowest-cost bulk water supply solution for the proposed mine, with a single abstraction point approximately 9 km south of the mine.
The mine developer has also explained that with the expected increase in the process plant throughput to 48 Mtpa, the project’s electricity requirements have increased accordingly.
The current power demand estimate is 260 MVA. Maximum demand and annual electricity consumption is estimated as 1.45 TWh, reflecting the larger scale of the operation and associated infrastructure requirements.
The Project’s power supply strategy remains centered on a connection to the NamPower grid, supplemented by solar photovoltaic (PV) generation and the integration of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to reduce overall energy costs and manage peak tariff periods.
Adding that the planned double-circuit 68km long 220 kV overhead transmission line from the Harib substation to the mine site remains a preferred and technically robust solution, and is expected to provide sufficient scalability to support the project’s long-term development plans.
As for the Environment and Social Impact Assessment and Environment Management Plan, which will support the Environmental Clearance Certificate application for the Mining License Area and Water Abstraction were submitted to MEFT on 19 August 2026 and 4 September respectively.
The decision is expected before the end of 2027.
All workstreams are on schedule to support PFS publication before the end of November 2026, the developer stated.
Koryx has also indicated that the plant layout has been finalised to optimise the use of the project terrain and minimise conveying distances, bulk earthworks, mine-to-crusher haul distances, utility requirements, and the overall footprint of processing and mining services.
“It also allows for future expansion through additional front-end and flotation circuits, should the project be expanded,” the statement revealed.
According to Koryx, Haib is a large copper porphyry deposit in southern Namibia with significant gold and molybdenum credits and a long history of exploration and project development by multiple operators.
Namibia is one of Africa’s most established mining jurisdictions with more than 120 years of continuous mining history and active mines in diamonds, uranium, gold, and copper.

articles.title: Chinese $6B Battery Investment in Morocco Reshapes EU Lithium Demand Amid Tariff Shifts - Shanghai Metals Market
articles.summary: Chinese $6B Battery Investment in Morocco Reshapes EU Lithium Demand Amid Tariff Shifts  Shanghai Metals Market
articles.full_text:
Chinese companies have announced US$6 billion of investment in battery and EV component plants in Morocco, where locally built cars are not exposed to the EU's additional duties on China made EVs. At the same time, lithium carbonate futures fell to their lowest level since December 2025 on concerns over the demand outlook, raising the question of where future battery-grade lithium demand will be located and how fast it will grow.
EU duties target China-built EVs, while Moroccan production avoids them
China now makes more than seven in ten of the world's electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million EVs, of which 1.25 million were exported, mainly to Europe. In the same year, the EU imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese EVs, on top of an existing 10% import tariff, as part of a system of tariffs and rules meant to protect an auto industry on which 13 million jobs depend. The measures have so far produced limited results, as Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025. Much of that volume is being driven by production in Morocco, where Chinese firms producing cars avoid exposure to the EU tariffs.
Morocco produced 560,000 vehicles in 2024, but only around 50,000 were electric
Morocco was already a significant automotive base. Cars are its biggest export, and Renault and Stellantis together form a manufacturing base that exported US$17 billion in cars and parts in 2024, making Morocco one of the EU's largest automotive trading partners, ahead of China. Of the 560,000 vehicles produced in 2024, the vast majority were petrol and diesel models, and only around 50,000, or about 9%, were electric. Stellantis and Renault have made multi-billion-euro commitments to expand EV and hybrid capacity, while Chinese investment is filling gaps in cathode and battery cell production.
Free zones, ports and trade agreements underpin investment; supply of battery minerals is partial
The government has spent two decades building free zones, areas where businesses can import, manufacture, process and re-export goods without paying normal taxes or customs duties, including automotive clusters such as the Tanger automotive city. The deep-water port in Tangier is the largest in Africa and the Mediterranean. Morocco has a free trade agreement with the EU and is the only North African country with one with the US. This year it introduced a carbon tax to keep its exports compliant with EU rules. On raw materials, Morocco holds around 70% of the world's phosphate reserves and a supply of cobalt, both relevant to battery production. Lithium reserves are not mentioned in the source material, and no source of lithium supply for the planned plants has been disclosed.
Transit hub or full industrialisation: policy and technology uncertainties remain
Whether Morocco benefits from the investment depends on what kind of production Chinese firms undertake. They could use Morocco as a transit hub with minimal processing, and the EU ruled in 2025 that aluminium wheels shipped from Morocco were being unfairly subsidised by Beijing. Alternatively, they could build full factories, share technology, train local engineers and buy from local suppliers, which is the type of industrialisation the African Union wants to encourage. Three uncertainties stand in the way: the EU's tariffs on Chinese electric cars are set for only five years and already face legal challenges, the technology may remain in Chinese hands, and the geopolitical and climate context is volatile enough that business plans could change quickly.
Lithium carbonate futures fall to a nearly 10-month low on the China-EU hybrid car deal
On October 12, the most active lithium carbonate contract on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange touched 104,680 yuan/mt, its lowest since December 17, 2025, and ended daytime trade at 104,740 yuan/mt, down 11.8%, the steepest daily fall since March. The fall followed a deal between China and the EU that could cut Chinese hybrid car exports to the bloc by more than half, according to European Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič. Orient Securities analysts said the deal was better than earlier expectations of EU tariff hikes, but that China's export growth to the EU will slow afterwards. Prices are down by half from the 33-month high of 209,880 yuan/mt reached on May 13, amid concerns over the 2027 demand outlook. On the supply side, CATL's Jianxiawo mine has not yet restarted, and intermittent speculation about a restart has affected sentiment. Shares of Tianqi Lithium and Ganfeng Lithium fell 5.1% and 3.9% respectively.
Overseas battery capacity could add a new lithium demand node, but volumes are undisclosed
Chinese-backed cathode and cell plants are being built in Morocco, and Morocco's EV output is currently a small share of its vehicle production. Once operating, such plants would consume lithium chemicals, but no capacity or start dates have been disclosed, so the volume cannot be sized. Morocco could become an additional destination for battery-grade lithium outside China, partly offsetting the loss of direct vehicle export volume to the EU, though its effect on lithium prices cannot be quantified. The October 12 price move was driven by the China-EU hybrid deal, not by Morocco. Overall, the Moroccan build-out sits between trade policy that limits China's vehicle exports and a lithium market weighed down by 2027 demand concerns. Over the coming months, the capacity and timing of the Moroccan cathode and cell plants, the outcome of the legal challenges to the EU tariffs, and the 2027 demand outlook will be key indicators for assessing lithium demand and prices.

Cornish Metals PLC (AIM:TIN) has launched a proposed £135 million fundraising to advance its South Crofty tin mine in Cornwall towards first production in mid-2028, securing backing from commodities giant Glencore alongside a six-year agreement to purchase the mine's output.
The fundraising, priced at 60p per share, includes an approximately £11.2 million investment from Glencore, which has agreed to purchase 100% of South Crofty's tin concentrate production for six years from the start of commercial operations. The agreement covers a minimum aggregate delivery volume of 27,513 metric tonnes of contained tin.

The equity raise is a crucial step towards unlocking US$210 million of previously secured bond financing, currently held in escrow. Cornish Metals must raise at least US$161 million in equity by 21 November to satisfy a key condition for accessing those funds.
Together with existing cash, the financing forms part of a £302 million funding plan, including £185 million earmarked for South Crofty's development.
Chief executive Don Turvey said the funding would allow the company to "accelerate development activities while securing the remaining long-lead items essential for the project's delivery."
"The strength and calibre of our expanded shareholder register, together with the oversubscribed debt financing announced in May, demonstrate the strategic importance of the South Crofty project to both the UK and the wider Western critical minerals supply chain," Turvey commented.
