articles.title: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction - CNBC
articles.summary: Copper is outshining gold this year. Investors say the rally can survive an AI correction  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Copper is becoming increasingly strategic to governments and industries as artificial intelligence, power-grid investment and defense spending increase demand for the industrial metal, investors say.
The metal — a key component in electronics, construction and transportation, and often seen as a barometer of economic activity — has outperformed gold this year, as the need to secure reliable supplies has intensified.
Copper has rallied 15.8% year-to-date, and is up more than 30% over the past 12 months. By comparison, gold futures have slipped 4.11% year-to-date, and are down 4.52% over the past 12 months. Spot gold is 4.89% lower over the past 12 months, and 4% down year-to-date.
Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe," Ivanhoe Electric CEO Taylor Melvin said countries, regions and industries are increasingly focused on securing access to metals for national security, economic growth and technology infrastructure. Melvin said that shift has helped support copper prices.
"It's certainly a good time to be in copper mining globally, and specifically in the United States," said Melvin, whose Arizona-based mining and exploration company focuses on copper, gold, silver, nickel and cobalt.
"We're really in a world right now where the metals that we used to refer to, and still do, as critical metals are really becoming strategic metals, in every sense of the word," said Melvin, who spoke as LME Week, the annual gathering of the global metals industry, began in London on Monday.
That shift comes as investors question the sustainability of AI spending and the hyperscaler build-out, which has led to a recent wobble in tech stocks.
But Melvin said he expects copper to withstand the recent volatility.
"It's a new pocket of demand, and it really is almost an inelastic demand for copper," he said of the tech sector's need for the metal. "It's hard to think that one of these large-scale technology companies is going to make an investment decision on a hyperscale data center based on the cost of copper."
He added: "That same inelasticity applies to another demand pocket that's emerging, which is national security, national defense budgets. So when you look at copper demand, the impact of technology, artificial intelligence infrastructure, I think we can all agree that that market is growing.
"There certainly has been a bit of a retrench, a retreat, in those [tech] valuations. But two things can be true at the same time — you can have a capital market move in sentiment on equity values… but it can also be true that those industries are growing, and they're going to be a source of incremental demand for our metal."
The rally has also been supported by uncertainty over whether the U.S. will impose a tariff on refined copper. In 2025, the Commerce Department recommended a 15% tariff beginning Jan. 1, 2027, but no final decision on the proposed levy has been publicly announced.
"Because of the potential for US tariffs, a large share of the world's copper is now stored in the U.S., and it isn't clear those stocks will be available to the rest of the market," said Iain Pyle, senior investment director at Aberdeen Investments and co-manager of the abrdn Future Minerals Fund.
"At the same time, Chinese inventories look exceptionally low and premiums there are rising."
In an Oct. 15 note, Pyle called copper the "clearest example" of a market where supply cannot keep up with demand. "Higher incentives will be needed in the form of sustained higher copper prices.
"There is still some risk of a pullback around tariff announcements, but we see the underlying fundamentals as clearly bullish, and the potential for a spike in prices has increased."

articles.title: Is Sandfire Resources (ASX:SFR) a Casualty of Copper Nerves? - Kalkine Media
articles.summary: Is Sandfire Resources (ASX:SFR) a Casualty of Copper Nerves?  Kalkine Media
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Sandfire Resources shares slipped again on Tuesday and are weaker over the past week.
- Copper sentiment has been rattled by a Chilean strike that has ended and doubts over technology spending.
- The company's assets in Spain, Botswana and Western Australia leave it tied closely to the copper price.
Sandfire Resources (ASX:SFR) Basic Materials Sandfire Resources Ltd (ASX:SFR) 20.06 AUD -0.260 1.280% Last Updated at: 2026-10-21T04:10:00Z shares eased again on Tuesday and have lost ground across the past week, as the mid-tier copper producer ended up caught in a wave of caution across the metals complex. The slide follows a period in which copper prices wobbled on supply and demand signals, leaving pure-play producers more exposed than the diversified giants. Sandfire Resources is a constituent of the ASX 200. The update is a notable talking point across ASX Metal and Mining Stocks.
A rough week for a copper pure play
Sandfire Resources moved lower in morning trade on Tuesday as materials led the local market down, and the stock has now surrendered a meaningful slice of value across the week. Peers with heavy copper exposure have experienced similar pressure.
Because the company has no large iron ore or coal arm to cushion earnings, its shares tend to track the copper price more closely than those of the larger miners. When sentiment sours, the effect is amplified.
For context, the producer's market value has swung widely over recent years, rising on the back of the Motheo build and falling when copper cooled. That sensitivity is the price of being a focused copper company in a market that rewards diversification during rough patches.
What is driving copper sentiment
a couple of forces have pulled in opposite directions. A strike at a major Chilean mine, which had raised fears about supply, ended last week, easing the tightness that had supported prices. At the same time, questions about how much money the technology sector will spend on artificial intelligence have clouded the demand picture for data-centre wiring and power equipment.
Copper rose on the London Metal Exchange on Monday, yet it had fallen across the previous week. That kind of choppy behaviour makes it hard for smaller producers to find a clear direction.
Traders also watch the relationship between copper and the Australian dollar, since the company reports in United States dollars but is listed locally. A firmer local currency can blunt the benefit of higher metal prices, adding another moving part to the earnings picture.
The MATSA operation in Spain
Sandfire's biggest producing asset is the MATSA complex in Spain's Iberian Pyrite Belt, comprising several underground mines and a large processing plant. It produces copper, zinc and lead concentrates, so by-product credits help offset costs when base metals trade firmly.
Motheo and the Kalahari Copper Belt
The Motheo project in Botswana is the company's growth platform. It sits in the Kalahari Copper Belt, a region that has drawn considerable exploration interest as explorers search for the next large sediment-hosted deposit.
DeGrussa legacy and exploration
Sandfire initial built its reputation on DeGrussa in the Bryah Basin of Western Australia, a high-grade copper-gold mine that delivered strong cash flow and funded the company's international expansion. The original operation has matured, though the surrounding province still receives exploration attention.
Reading earlier copper-driven falls
This is not the earliest time copper nerves have hit the stock. In September a fall in copper prices dragged Sandfire lower on a Friday, alongside a Canadian peer, in a move attributed purely to the metal's price rather than company news.
Placing Sandfire in the market
Sandfire is a member of the ASX 200, so it tends to feature in sector baskets and exchange-traded funds that track resources. That brings steady liquidity and also correlated moves when funds adjust their allocation to materials.
Wider coverage of ASX Metal and Mining Stocks illustrates how broad the selection of listed producers has become, from iron ore giants to gold and lithium names, and how differently each reacts to the same macro headline.
The stock's liquidity is healthy, and it features in several resource-focused funds. That ensures a constant flow of orders, and it also means short bursts of fund rebalancing can move the price in the absence of any company news.
Balance sheet and capital priorities
Growth in Botswana and Spain has been funded through a mix of operating cash flow and debt facilities. With copper prices near the middle of recent ranges, the group has room to service obligations, but any prolonged weakness would tighten the picture.
Management has emphasised cost discipline and the reliability of MATSA, which provides a steady base. The balance between debt reduction and further growth spending will be a recurring topic as the project pipeline matures.
Financial flexibility will matter if the copper price stays soft. Operating cash flow from MATSA offers a base, while scheduled debt repayments and growth commitments will determine how much room remains for new projects.
The long-term copper case
Despite near-term volatility, the structural argument for copper remains widely discussed. Electrification of transport, expansion of power grids and renewable energy installations all require large quantities of the metal, while new mine supply is slow and expensive to bring online.
What to watch from here
The next catalysts include the quarterly production report, due in the coming weeks, which will show how MATSA and Motheo performed through the September period. Market participants will look for throughput, grades and unit costs.
Beyond company news, copper inventories, Chinese demand data and the direction of the United States dollar will probably set the tone. Until those signals settle, the shares are likely to remain sensitive to every move in the metal.
Seasonal factors in Spain and southern Africa are modest, but weather, power supply and logistics can still produce uneven results from quarter to quarter, which is why the market treats each production report with care.

Copper prices remained volatile during the third quarter of 2026 as mining disruptions and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continued to constrain supply.
Copper prices climbed to record highs in Q3 as the market stayed tight.
Expectations of US tariffs on refined copper drove momentum, drawing metal into Comex warehouses and draining stocks from overseas warehouses controlled by the London Metal Exchange (LME) and the Shanghai Futures Exchange (SHFE). However, movements cooled in September after the White House said it had not made a final decision.
The ongoing conflict between the US and Iran also affected copper prices, driving up producer costs, most notably through supply constraints for sulfuric acid. Likewise, mine supply continued to be impacted by reduced output at the Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula mines as they recovered from significant shutdowns in 2025.
On the demand side, data centers and the energy transition are adding to base-level growth from urbanization in the Global South and grid upgrades worldwide. Looking ahead, attention is turning to forecasts of a widening supply deficit.
What happened to the copper price in Q3?
Copper prices were volatile at the start of Q3, but largely saw upward momentum, starting at US$6.18 per pound on July 1, and rising over the course of the month to close at US$6.47 on the Comex on July 31.
Copper price, July 1 to October 19, 2026.
Chart via the Investing News Network.
High trading volumes pushed prices from US$6.54 on August 3 to US$6.69 on August 31.
Comex copper hit a fresh all-time high on September 9, climbing to US$6.89. While prices retreated as the quarter closed, they remained elevated compared to the rest of the year, closing September 30 at US$6.62.
Prices also rose in London, with the standard three month contract on the LME on an upward trajectory for the quarter, rising from US$13,298.50 per metric ton (MT) on July 1 to US$14,410 on September 30.
Copper prices hit a new LME record on September 9 as well, reaching an intraday high of US$14,858, beating the previous record of US$14,527 set on January 29.
Tariff fears pull copper into US warehouses
US trade policy was the biggest single driver of copper prices in Q3.
When copper tariffs were first implemented in 2025, refined copper was spared, but recommended phased levies were set at 15 percent starting in January 2027 and rising to 30 percent in 2028. US traders have accelerated domestic stockpiling for that reason, with larger quantities of refined product reaching domestic warehouses.
The movements have created a premium, making it more profitable to buy copper on the LME and ship it into the US. This dynamic pushed imports into American warehouses to a record 225,094 MT in July.
By October 13, Comex inventories stood at approximately 787,616 short tons.
Inventories elsewhere fell sharply during the quarter.
LME warehouse inventories sank to 231,275 MT on October 9, down from 324,850 MT on June 30. Likewise, SHFE stocks had fallen more than 80 percent since March, hitting 69,731 MT by mid-August.
In an email to the Investing News Network (INN), SP Angel partner and mining analyst John Meyer explained that despite declines in inventory, demand outside the US remains robust.
“We believe demand in China for copper remains strong. News suggests China is still buying up available physical copper. We feel visible inventories are more representative than they have been for many years with high process attracting metal into LME warehouses from cheaper storage locations,” he commented.
The White House acknowledged that it had received recommendations from the Department of Commerce on June 30 regarding whether tariffs should be implemented on refined copper starting on January 1, 2027.
A decision was widely expected by September; however, Reuters reported on September 10 that no decision had been made; that caused rising copper prices to stabilize through the end of the quarter.
Shanghai Metals Market notes that until the White House rules out refined copper tariffs, copper inventories are likely to remain tied to the US, with room for renewed inflows if the Comex premium widens.
Middle East war drives up producer costs
The Iran war continued to raise input costs for copper producers in Q3, though pressure on sulfuric acid eased late in the quarter. Solvent extraction and electrowinning operations, which account for 22 percent of global mined copper output, rely on sulfuric acid to leach copper from oxide ore, and the Middle East is a key source of the sulfur it requires.
Chile, the world’s top copper producer, has been particularly exposed.
Spot acid prices at the Chilean port of Mejillones doubled to US$380 per MT in April, and China, which supplied 37.1 percent of Chile’s acid imports in 2025, restricted exports in May.
However, there were signs of relief by the end of Q3. China sent its first acid shipment to Chile since May at 32,000 MT, though it covers only a fraction of Chile’s needs, and acid prices have eased since peaking in Q2.
Diesel, the other major cost pressure for open-pit mines, has also been trading near record prices through much of the third quarter. The fuel powers haul trucks and other heavy equipment essential to mine operations.
Earlier in the year, Codelco said higher diesel and supply costs would add roughly 10 cents per pound to its cash costs, an increase of about 5 percent. While President Donald Trump said in October that the US had cut a deal with Russia to provide the market with diesel, analysts suggest the quantities are too small to significantly impact prices.
            
                Copper supply disruptions continue
Copper mine supply stayed constrained in the third quarter. The two major operations that shut down in 2025 are still recovering, and new risks emerged in Chile and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).
At Freeport-McMoRan's (NYSE:FCX) Grasberg mine in Indonesia, mill throughput averaged about 140,000 MT of ore per day in Q3, roughly 67 percent of normal rates before the September 2025 mud rush. Freeport expects to reach 80 percent of capacity in mid-2027 and near full capacity by the end of 2027. Meanwhile, at Ivanhoe Mines' (TSX:IVN,OTCQX:IVPAF) Kamoa-Kakula mine in DRC, copper production ticked up to 76,401 MT in Q3, up from 64,328 MT in Q2. Ivanhoe said 2026 output is trending toward the low end of its 290,000 to 310,000 MT guidance.
It's worth noting that in August, the DRC banned copper concentrate exports to support domestic processing.
However, the impact is expected to be limited, with the biggest effects felt in Zambia, which processes most of the raw copper the DRC exports. The majority of DRC’s copper exports consist of refined copper products, and Kamoa-Kakula’s concentrate is now smelted in the country.
“DRC copper concentrate used to go to Zambia for smelting, and I suspect some still does. Am sure cobalt still leaks out of the DRC,” Meyer said.
            
                Strike threats in Chile
Labor talks broke down at two major Chilean mines in late September.
At Antofagasta's (LSE:ANTO,OTCPL:ANFGF) Centinela, which produced 240,400 MT of copper in 2025, two unions representing 708 workers voted 98.73 percent to strike. Although the workers took to the picket lines on October 7, Antofagasta is maintaining its full-year output forecast.
Days after the Centinela strike vote, 95 percent of participating members for the supervisors' union at BHP's (ASX:BHP,NYSE:BHP,LSE:BHP) Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, rejected the company’s final contract offer. The vote came after a worker at the mine was killed in a maintenance-related accident on September 23.
BHP requested government mediation, effectively halting any potential worker job action. On October 13, the company and union representatives reached a tentative agreement that included improved benefits and will be presented to union workers for ratification. The deal averts a walkout that could have potentially come that same day.
In an interview with INN on the sidelines of the Precious Metals Summit, McEwen Copper Managing Director Michael Meding said these incidents point to structural deficits in the copper market.
“Some of the most important mines have been hit with unfortunate events, whether that is Grasberg, whether that's Kamoa, whether there that been Cobre Panama,” he said. While he noted that these incidents are only temporary, Meding also raised a more serious issue: declining grades at some of the world’s largest mines.
Meyer echoed that point, suggesting it’s the more serious problem facing copper’s supply side.
“Almost all supply disruptions are temporary. In Chile it was storms, but a fall off in grades is a more permanent issue. In Indonesia, Grasberg is coming back to capacity, albeit slowly. The DRC will always have issues,” he said.

articles.summary: Battery Age Minerals (ASX:BM8) Advances Lithium and Germanium Exploration Across Three Continents  Kalkine
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- Battery Age Minerals (ASX:BM8) expanded the Falcon Lake lithium land package to approximately 60 square kilometres in July 2026.
- Falcon Lake drilling previously intersected 54.1 metres grading 1.74% lithium oxide in hole 24FL-107.
- The company completed a germanium-related technology licensing agreement with NTUitive in June 2026.
- The exploration portfolio spans lithium in Canada, germanium and gallium in the United States, and critical minerals in Austria.
Battery Age Minerals Limited (ASX:BM8) is an Australian-listed mineral explorer pursuing lithium and other critical minerals projects across several jurisdictions. Its recent disclosures have focused on extending the Falcon Lake lithium footprint in Ontario and developing a broader germanium and gallium strategy that combines exploration with technology access. The company's September 2026 annual report also provides a reference point for reviewing its exploration-stage business and funding requirements. At the time of writing on 19 October 2026, Battery Age Minerals shares were trading at AUD 0.034, down 10.53% during the day's trading session.
Company Business
Battery Age's Falcon Lake project lies within Ontario's Caribou Lake-O'Sullivan greenstone belt in Canada. The company explores spodumene-bearing pegmatites and evaluates lithium alongside other reported critical minerals. Its portfolio also includes the Apex germanium-gallium project in Utah, United States, and the Bleiberg project in Austria. These assets expose the business to different geological settings, permitting systems and exploration schedules rather than to an established production stream.
At Falcon Lake, mineral exploration is directed at mapping pegmatites, testing extensions to known mineralised zones and identifying future drill targets. At Apex and Bleiberg, the work is directed toward assessing germanium, gallium and associated mineral potential. The company also reported exploration activity at its El Aguila project, including gold and silver drilling results earlier in 2026. The geographic spread creates multiple work programs but also requires disciplined allocation of exploration expenditure.
Recent Development
In July 2026, Battery Age announced that it had staked another 46 mineral claims at Falcon Lake, adding approximately nine square kilometres and extending its tenure around seven kilometres east. The expanded landholding was reported at approximately 60 square kilometres. The company said the newly acquired claims would be included in its prospecting and geochemical sampling plans. That work was intended to prioritise targets for follow-up exploration rather than establish a new mineral resource.
Previously reported Falcon Lake drilling included 54.1 metres at 1.74% lithium oxide from 100.85 metres down-hole in drillhole 24FL-107 and 55.95 metres at 1.47% lithium oxide from 222.2 metres in 24FL-108. These are drill intersections, not production results or estimates of economically recoverable material. The company has also disclosed assays for rubidium, caesium, tantalum and gallium, which broaden the geological questions being evaluated at the property.
Separately, in June 2026 the company announced completion of an exclusive patent and know-how licence agreement with NTUitive, the commercialisation entity of Nanyang Technological University in Singapore. It followed an earlier evaluation arrangement and forms part of Battery Age's germanium strategy. The company also reported satellite analysis identifying priority germanium-gallium targets at Apex and continued technical and permitting work relevant to the Austrian Bleiberg project.
Financial Performance and Sector Context
Battery Age remains principally an exploration business, making cash availability, funding access and exploration spending more informative operating measures than mining output. The company published its FY26 annual report in September 2026 and an amended June-quarter Appendix 5B cash-flow report in July. Investors assessing its financial position can monitor the cash balance, payments for exploration and administration, and the extent to which proposed programs can be funded from existing resources. Production revenue, EBITDA from mining operations and mine output should not be inferred from drilling activity.
The portfolio is exposed to differing commodity markets. Lithium exploration economics depend partly on prices for battery raw materials, while germanium and gallium projects face distinct demand, processing and supply-chain conditions. Early-stage discoveries also require metallurgical assessment, additional drilling and potentially resource estimation before development economics can be evaluated. Battery Age's cross-border activities introduce currency, jurisdictional and logistical considerations alongside those commodity-specific issues.
Risks to Consider
Exploration results may not translate into a mineral resource or a commercially viable mine. The timing and outcome of field programs depend on access, permits, weather, contractors and laboratory processing. New claim areas can require further geological evidence before drilling decisions are made. Germanium-related technology licensing likewise does not by itself establish a commercial processing operation. Ongoing exploration, corporate expenditure and possible project studies may require fresh capital, which could dilute existing shareholdings if equity is issued.
What to Watch Next
Near-term monitoring points include the company's next quarterly activities and cash-flow disclosures, results from Falcon Lake mapping and geochemical programs, and any updates on drill-target selection. At Apex, the progression of priority targets from remote-sensing interpretation to field evaluation will be relevant. For Bleiberg, permitting and exploration planning remain matters to follow. Further statements about the NTUitive agreement may clarify technical testing arrangements and how the licensed technology is intended to fit within the wider strategy.
Key Insights
Battery Age entered the latter part of 2026 with an enlarged Canadian lithium landholding and exploration programs spanning lithium, germanium, gallium and other minerals. Its disclosed Falcon Lake intercepts provide geological data, while the new claims increase the area requiring assessment. The NTUitive licence adds a technology component to its germanium plans, but commercial outcomes remain unestablished. Funding capacity, verified exploration results, permits and the sequencing of field work will determine what further evidence becomes available to evaluate the portfolio.
